Dr. Bruce, of course, wanted the very best doctors that could be obtained, and there was no necessity, so far as I can see, for keeping unfit or incompetent doctors in the service at that stage. I was greatly impressed by a letter published in the Toronto Globe recently from Adelaide R. Poole, R.N., who had been a nurse for a year and a half in military hospitals in France and England. I do not know the lady, but I should like to read one paragraph of her letter:
But the whole thing goes deeper than mere details of rival reports. The offence for which Col. Bruce is being punished is that he, being a doctor, dared to criticise other doctors. He dared, as a man acting in the interests of the public, to do his duty, even although it involved his sinning against medical etiquette, and consequently, no matter whether he be right or wrong, he has, and will have, almost the whole medical- profession against him. This is the root of the whole matter, and the short-sighted public, instead of standing by the man who, for their sakes, broke one of the strongest fetishes of our day, join in the cry against him.
This decision, this disqualification of a man who did his duty as he saw it, will have a far deeper effect than most people realize. Even at the present time, medical etiquette is so strong in military hospitals, that a Colonel, an old and

experienced doctor, will hesitate before interfering with the youngest medical officer's treatment of a case, even when he feels in his heart it is mistaken, and will shut his eyes to habits and incompetence, in a way that could happen in no other corps in the army. Thinking people feel there is a danger to the community, even in civil life, in the way one doctor stands by another, no matter how inefficient or unworthy of confidence he be. No one but another member of the profession can say a doctor has made a mistake, or done wrong, no matter how flagrant the case may be. The patient is generally dead, the friends and relatives are ignorant, and the nurse, even when she knows, is trained not to speak. But after this lesson, an efficient, conscientious doctor, when he knows things are wrong in a hospital, knows lives are imperiled or lost by the habits of incompetence of other men, sometimes inferior to him in rank, though he break his heart over it, will keep quiet lest worse befall liim-lest he himself be deprived of his chance of being useful. He will do his own work, and shut his eyes to what goes on around him. And he will be wise.
If a man appointed and paid to inspect is punished and dismissed for making a real report on what he finds, instead of patting every one on the back, as is usually the case, what would happen to just an ordinary officer if he dared to speak? If the public stand for it, they deserve what will come to them. But what of the helpless soldiers?
That is written by an experienced nurse who knows what is going on in some of these hospitals. I have no desire to make things seem worse than they are, but I should like some explanation from the minister as to why the department deserted Dr. Bruce wdien he was attempting to perform a very important public duty.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not think it is correct to say that the department deserted Dr. Bruce. Dr. Bruce made a certain report which aroused a good deal of controversy. The subject was investigated by another board, and the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sinclair) seems to be under the impression that that board was composed of one British officer, and that Canada was not represented on it at all; at least, if he is not under that impression himself, he conveyed that impression to the committee. The board was composed of Surgeon-General Sir William Babtie, K.C.M.G., C.B., V.C.; Colonel E. C. Ashton, G.O.C., C.T.D., Shorncliffe; Colonel J. T. Eother-ingham, C.M.G., A.D.M.S., 2nd Canadian Division, B.E.F.; Colonel A. E. Ross, C.M.G., A.D.M.S., 1st Canadian Division,
B.E.F.; Lieutenant-Colonel J. M. Elder, No. 3 Canadian Hospital, Boulogne. I do not believe you could find four names in the medical profession in Canada that would command greater respect than those.
Dr. Bruce was not a member of the second board?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, but I understand he was present and had the opportunity of making representations.
He says not. He says he was called to give evidence, but was not permitted to attend the sittings of the board.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I understand he was permitted to make his representations to the board. He may not have been permitted to attend their deliberations, but that is a somewhat different thing from what I stated.
So far as the medical service overseas is concerned, it is under the direction of a gentleman whom I believe to be a very competent officer. I saw something of him and heard a good deal about him when I was there this year. Surgeon-General Foster is a gerjjleman who has had considerable experience in the Canadian permanent service. He went across the Atlantic early in the war, and has had the advantage of a wide experience over there, and when new arrangements were made nearly a year ago, he was selected for the position which he now holds, namely, head of the Canadian Medical Services overseas. I believe he is discharging his duties efficiently and well, and that the services are being efficiently conducted. Of course, the experience of a person who visits hospitals and sees the patients is not by any means conclusive, but in justice to the management of the Canadian hospitals overseas, and in justice to the management of the British hospitals which I visited-and I visited a great (many-I am bound to say this: although I inquired very frequently, indeed of almost every man whom I saw in the hospitals, whether they had any cause for complaint or any suggestion or representation to make, I never heard from fir^t to last in the. thirty or forty hospitals I visited in March and April of this year, a single complaint from a Canadian patient, or for that matter, from any patient, and I never saw anything in any one of these hospitals that would call for a critical remark. The men all seemed to be well eared for, comfortable and contented. As far as I could judge everything that could be devised for their care and comfort had been done.
As far as the V.A.D. hospitals are concerned, there are none of these at present under the Canadian system. There are some, however, under the British..system and I visited some of these, but I saw

nothing to excite criticism or comment on their management. I should be very sorry to believe that the Canadians who have gone overseas and have been wounded in this war or are suffering from illness are not being properly cared for; I believe that they are.
The work of the Canadian Army Medical Corps in the fight at Vimy Eidge has been described to me and it indicated a remark-, able degree of efficiency. The arrangements for moving back the wounded and caring for them at once were remarkably thorough, and there was nothing left undone that one could suggest. I remember reading a letter quite recently from a Canadian physician who went overseas about two years ago. Dr. Andrew McPhail, of McGill University. The letter was not written to me, but to a friend who showed it to me. I am sorry I have not it here to read to the committee because it would impress upon the committee the splendid efficiency of the arrangements that were carried out by the Canadian Army Medical Service in that battle. Those arrangements reflect the highest credit upon every one concerned in them. The arrangements were thought out just as carefully, so far as they concerned the care of the wounded, as any of the other operations. When, in Ithe midst of the fight, through sudden change in weather conditions, it became necessary to have 600 or 800 additional blankets brought up immediately, although that call was absolutely unexpected, those blankets were provided within less than one hour. The arrangements from first to last struck me as indicating the highest degree of efficiency in the care of our wounded at the front, as disclosed by what took place during and after that battle. With the profound conviction I have that the Army Medical Service in the Canadian Expeditionary Force is thoroughly efficient, I would deeply regret that the impression should get abroad through this country from anything said in this committee that the reverse is the case. I am convinced that the men who are serving in the Army Medical Service of the Canadian Expeditionary Force are not only .men of excellent knowledge and wide experiences, but that they are men animated by the highest devotion to duty. They have not spared themselves in this war. They have gone to the very firing line whenever necessary. There have been many casualties among them. I have seen their ambulances with scores of shrapnel and bullet marks on them. Those men are 252
right out in the very midst of the fighting, whenever it is necessary that they should be there. They do not stay behjnd. They and the orderlies under them go forward to where the wounded men -are lying. I believe these men are doing as good service for Canada and the Empire to-day as any men in the Expeditionary Force, and that too much credit cannot be given to them for the .splendid spirit by which they are inspired and the splendid work they have done.

I fully appreciate the
remarks the Prime Minister has made. It is not in the mind of any one here to question the fact that the Army Service Corps is one of the best in the world. We all know they are doing splendid work. As the Premier has said, they are performing the most wonderful service. They take their chances along with the rest of the soldiers. But, if I understand it, the Bruce and the Babtie reports which are now under discussion do not refer in any way to this. The only thing those reports refer to is the treatment of the wounded in the hospitals in England, and the point is, is that right or is it wrong? The Premier eays that he Ghould be very sorry to see any doubt east upon the service 5 p.m. in this committee. But when we come to consider the Bruce and the Babtie reports, I ask this committee if it would not be well to set the whole matter before the people, and have the reports placed on the Table go that we may know where we are. It has appeared to me for some weeks, as it must have struck many members of this committee, that there is an air of mystery which should not exist concerning this affair. It should not 'be so, as a matter of right to the Canadian people' who are entitled to know what is being done so far as their relatives and their wounded are concerned. And the reason why the matter should be cleared up is that if this state of mystery continues it will not help recruiting. Ae I understand it, Dr. Bruce is one of the most eminent men of his profession, not only on this continent, but probably one of the most eminent to be found anywhere. On account of the alleged existence of certain conditions in England, he was sent to make a report. In one of the paragraphs of his report he says:
In view of the unanimity of my confreres who contributed in so important a measure to my report, may I briefly outline their eminent qualifications for the unpleasant but necessary task which they so cheerfully and ably performed.



Then he gives the names:	Col. Reid,
Col. Wallace Scott, Col. Wilson and Col. Walter McKeown. I do not know any of these men, and I have not the faintest idea who they may be; but, knowing the reputation Dr. Bruce holds in this country, and knowing the class of man he is, I am perfectly satisfied he did not take these men with him for the sake of making a biased report. He took them for the purpose of helping him to do the work he was sent to do. He consulted them, and they brought in a report finding, as my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) has shown, 23 grounds upon which the Canadian hospitals are no.t being properly administered, and making 23 recommendations as to how these wrongs may be righted. In their report they say: Do these things, in order that conditions may be bettered. Then what happens? Col. Babtie goes over, taking certain eminent medical men with him, and he makes a report in contradistinction to the Bruce, report, and says that in certain things Bruce is all wrong, and Babtie is all right. You have it on the Prime Minister's own admission that Col. Babtie is a most eminent medical man. You have not only the admission of the Prime Minister that he is an eminent medical man, but the English Government has said so, because they put him in charge of one of the most difficult medical transport services they had; and, eminent though he was, he sofentirely failed that the English Government have practically had to take the matter in hand and censure him. We have the Bruce report, and we have the Babtie report, and in connection with this Babtie report, the man who made it has come to grief through want of real medical knowledge along the lines he took.
Then, Sir, we have the Jones report, and with that I shall not deal. But we have this fact, that Dr. Bruce, in all fairness, considering his reputation, whether as a medical man or as a citizen, having been criticized in the Babtie report, should have had the human right to reply and say wherein he was right and wherein General Babtie was wrong. Again the mystery-why, I know not-but for weeks we have been endeavouring to get that reply from Dr. Bruce so that we might argue the question out and find, at least to our own satisfaction, whether we are right or wrong. As I understand it, this second Bruce report seems to have vanished into thin air. The Minister of Militia says he sent it to 
the minister overseas. The minister overseas says he never got it.

What authority
has my hon. friend for that statement?

I have a letter here, written in the early part of this month by a man who had. seen the overseas minister [DOT]and the overseas minister says he nwer , got that report. That, I submit, is fairly good evidence. May I now ask if the minister has a copy of that report, and if he has, whether he will lay it on the table of the'House? May I expect an answer?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have already
given the answer. As far hack as the 31st tday I said:
It is not the intention of the Government to lay it on the Table without first submitting it to the overseas Minister of Militia to whom in the ordinary course it should be presented, as it relates to matters under his immediate jurisdiction. Whether or not the report will afterwards he laid upon the Table,
1 am not for the moment prepared to say. I speak not of my own knowledge when I refer to the contents of the report, because It is voluminous and I have not had time to read it hut I understand that a portion of it is not responsive to anything in the report of the Commission over which General Babtie presided and that it is not made in respect of any matter upon which Colonel Bruce was asked to report. Whether that is the case I am not now prepared to say, owing to lack or time to make the necessary examination. 1 am thoroughly of opinion, however, that the report should first be submitted to the Overseas Minister of Militia.
That is what I said on the 31st May, and that is the position to which I still adhere. If the minister of the overseas forces has not received it, I do not understand the reason for that, because the Minister of Militia and Defence forwarded it to him. It is possible that it may have gone down in some vessel sunk by a submarine, but we have no reason to suppose that such is the case. It is a proper suggestion that we should ascertain by cabling whether he has received it, and we shall do that.

I have never been a
member of a Government and so I am not familiar with the procedure of Governments, but I cannot understand, when the second Bruce report came, even although as the Prime Minister has said, it refers to matters that are within the knowledge of 'the 'minister overseas, why Sir George Per-ley should have to revise that report before it was given to the members of this House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I did not say
he ishould revise it.

Practically, th*e Prime
Minister agrees 'with me, because he says that, as the minister overseas has to do with matters, that are contained in the report, it ought to be .submitted to him. Am I rigiht in that,?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I say it should have been submitted to Mm in the first place.

Dr. Bruce was appointed by this Government to report on certain things. He was not .appointed by the minister overseas, but by order in council here, to report and give his findings. I submit that if he were to give an unbiased report he would go over there to report and without having reference, near or remote, to Sir George Parley, he would come hack with that report, and the Government should lay that report upon the table of the House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not think my hon. friend quite understands the situation. Colonel Bruce was not appointed by order in council. He was appointed by the then Minister of Militia and Defence to make inquiry and report. His report would naturally go to the Minister of Militia and Defence. It would not be sent to the Minister of Public Works or the Minister of the Naval Service; it would be sent to the minister who appointed him. After that report had been made, or about the time it was made, a change took place by which the duties that had up to that time been discharged by the Minister of Militia and Defence were divided, and in the future a portion of fcho.se duties were .to he discharged by the Minister of Militia and Defence, and a portion of the duties were to be discharged by the minister of the overseas service. The particular matters to which the report related came under the jurisdiction conferred upon the minister of the overseas service, and therefore, for that purpose, he ocupied the position which the Minister of Militia and Defence occupied in (the first instance. That is the reason why I say the report should have been presented to Sir George Perley in the first instance. I .should like to make this plain further to my hon. friend-we are speaking of this document as a report. It is not a report in the ordinary sense.
It is rather the criticisms or observations of Colonel Bruce in respect of the report made by the board of. which General Bab-tie was the president. It was not ask for by any minister or- by the Government; but he exercised his right, 252J
as he understood it, of making a reply to the conclusions that had been formulated in the report made by the board to which I have just alluded. So that, in the strict, technical sense, it is not a report but rather his reply to or observations upon the report made by that board.

Along that same line of * reasoning, may I submit to the minister that, as it was only comment upon the Babtie report, if it should not be submitted to this House, and if it was not a report proper, why should it be submitted to the Minister of Militia overseas? But the Prime Minister says that it was. As I understand, it is then in this position, that the second Bruce commentary or report, whatever we may desire to call it, was made in answe.r to the Babtie report, that that commentary upon the Babtie report was sent here, I suppose, to this Government, to the Minister of Militia, or to my right hon. friend.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It did not come to me.

Then the Minister of Militia no. doubt got it. It got to the Government somehow. Then, after it gets to the Government, the Government says that this is of such importance and it is such an integral part of the Babtie and Bruce reports, that, in order that the matter may be kept perfectly straight, .and as the minister overseas has to deal with these matters, and as these matters must not be submitted to the House of Commons or laid on the Table in the form of a commentary or report, we must send this to the minister overseas in order that it may have his "O.K."
Am I right up to that point?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I would not say absolutely right. I will explain the position as I understand it. We say it should be sent to the minister overseas, as it related to questions under his jurisdiction and as to which he takes the place of the Minister of Militia. It should go to him in the regular course, but it should go to him for another purpose. I have already pointed out that it was not in response to any request of the Government, or of the Minister of Militia and Defence, or of the minister of the overseas service that it was sent. It contains some matters perhaps relating to the Babtie report, and a good deal of matter, which as I understand, does not relate either to that, or any other report. I am so informed

by the Deputy Minister of Militia and Defence, who made a study of it, and made a report upon it to the Government. I jsay it should go to the minister of the overseas service in. order that he might consult his officers in regard to it. It might be *necessary to make some explanation or .statement. I should suppose the minister *<of the overseas service would submit that , commentary or criticism to Surgeon General Foster, who is at the head of the service over there, and .ask him whether any of these criticisms, whatever they .may be, are well founded, and if they are well founded what he proposes with regard to them. All that would seem to me to be a very proper and fair way of dealing with it. So, it was really sent to the minister of the overseas service, not to obtain .hie O.K., hut for the two reasons: First, because he is the proper minister to whom it should be addressed, and, second, because the matters to which it relates are under the supervision and direction of himself and his officers, and it ought to be submitted to his officers, if it contains any matter of a serious character, in order that we may learn what they have to say about it.

I will concede what the Prime Minister has said, for the sake of argument-that it ought to be submitted to the overseas minister, and to Surgeon General Foster, that it might go through the proper channel to be O.K.'d and sent back here. The great point is that it should be here, or we should have a copy. It is now two months since it was sent. I think my request a reasonable one when I ask that the report, commentary, or whatever name the Government might like to give it, be wired for at once, that it be brought hack, and placed upon the table of the House.
Of course this question has nothing to do with the treatment of the wounded men in France or Flanders; their initial treatment in those countries is the very best; the Army Medical Service Corps is one of the best in the world. But this deals with the treatment of the wounded in England. We should have the Bruce report with its recommendations, and the Babtie report with its counter recommendations, and the Jones' report, and the final analysis-if it may be taken to be the final analysis of Colonel Bruce. That report ought to be before us, and if it is not before us, we should find out why it is now in the hands of the minister overseas. We might have a day to discuss it, because I think it is of the utmost consequence. The effects may be very far-reaching. The relatives of 
those wounded soldiers are interested, and in order that their minds may be set at rest, and in order that recruiting may not have the least set back whatever, the question whether the Babtie report or the Bruce report is right should be settled.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We will telegraph to Sir George Perley and find out whether the document has reached him. We will also telegraph him with respect to his view in regard to laying the document upon the table of the House, with or without any observations which his officers may desire to make with regard to it.

The Prime Minister has said that the second report, or commentary, made by Dr. Bruce was not asked for by the Government. It is the unofficial report of an official investigation. If the Government did not ask for it-and the Government does not seem to want it would there be any impropriety in Dr. Bruce making his reply public himself?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am really not in a .position to answer that, because it might relate to matters that it would he undesirable for Colonel Bruce to make public. It might be an advantage to the enemy to know these things; iit might'be i& detriment to the public interest, and I should not like to answer my hon. friend.
Can the hon. Minister of Militia inform me if he has received .a cable from Dr. Bruce within the last few days, in regard to the second report, and the publication of it?
I received a cable from Dr. Brace about .a week or ten days ago, merely saying that he wished ito have the report laid on the Table, or to have it made public, or .something of .that kind.

The question as to the contest between Dr. Bruce .and Dr. Babtie is not of very much importance to the people of this country, but I .should like to know whether any reforms have been introduced by the department to right the abuses referred to in Dr. Bruce's report. He has .spoken of some very vital questions. I have the highest regard foT the Canadian Medical Service. I know of a great many men from my own province who volunteered to take part in that service, and I know that many of them are among the .pick of the medical men of that province. I .am not aware that we sent any incompetent doctors from the province of Nova Scotia, but it appears from Dr. Bruce's report, if

we can rely on it, that men have found their way info the service that were unfit for the *position. The question is of vital importance. The civilian can choose his own doctor. If .any of the hon. gentlemen around me require .a doctor they select the best they can find, if they are able to pay for the service; but the soldier has to take what is given him; he is under the direction of a certain doctor who is looking after the ward, and his life is involved in the competence of that doctor. He has no choice, and therefore it is >a question of the *most vital importance that the Government should not have doctors in the service who are not fit for the duties devolving upon them. This is what Hr. Bruce says in regard to that matter:
The personnel of the Canadian Army Medical Corps has been greatly hampered by the granting of commissions to medical men whose ability in civil life, and, in some cases, whose well-known habits were such as to reasonably preclude them from being honoured with a commission in the C.A.M.C.
It has been found on investigation that many of the officers who have been given commissions have been failures as medical men at home, or are over age, or are drug fiends, or addicted to alcoholism, and these officers are not only of little or no use as C.A.M.C. officers, but their presence on an overseas unit is a detriment to the efficiency of that corps.
That is very strong language. If that statement is true, we have men in the service who are drug fiends or who are addicted to alcohol-men who should not be in the service at all. Did the Government take any action with a view to getting rid of these incompetent doctors?

The member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) opened his remarks by stating that none of these doctors, so far as he knew, came from the part of the country which he represents. I can say the same thing with regard to the part of the country that I represent. So far as my knowledge goes, the same remark applies to the whole of Canada, with some few exceptions. No doubt some of these doctors who were addicted to drugs got overseas-I cannot speak definitely on that point. A few doctors, however, were sent back from the front- out of the very large number that went over. The very best medical men in the country are overseas. In Toronto there are scarcely enough doctors to do the work required in the ordinary practice of medicine. The very pick of our doctors went overseas; I am confident that no reflection can be made in general upon the medical profession in that regard.

Dr. Bruce does not reflect generally upon the doctors who went overseas; he says that certain doctors have been given commissions who are unfit for the service. The minister has not answered my question, which was: Has the department got rid of these doctors, or are they still in the service? It is not necessary to say that we have good doctors over there; we all know that some of the most eminent medical men in Canada are in the service. But we cannot assume that Dr. Bruce made up this report out of whole cloth; we cannot assume that there is no truth in his statement. Will the minister answer my question as to whether these men are still in the service?

I thought I had made myseP perfectly ole.aT; I intended to, at any rate. Courts of inquiry were held in respect to. certain doctors, a/nd those doctors who were found incompetent to carry on their work were -sent back to Can-ad a.
AfteT Dr. Bruce's report was put in?
That has nothing to do with Dr. Bruce's report.

This is a matter of very deep concern to the people of Canada. There have been between 75,000 and 100,000 casualties m oror Canadian forces, spread from the Atlantic to the Pacific. There is not a settlement, town ot village in Canada in which some member of the community has not suffered casualty at the front. When a discussion such as this is *brought forward at this time, it is very unsatisfactory to the people of Canada who are interested to' find that, instead of the Government standing up and saying what they have done specifically to cure the conditions set forth in Dr. Bruce's report, the minister makes a general statement that things were not good, hut that now they are better; thalt they are not good in the service of other countries, and that we cannot expect to have them any better in 'Canada. That, I submit, is not a satisfactory answer, and it is not made any better Iby the defence of the Prime Minister thiat the medical service at the front is 'beyond question. The medical service at the front is not under consideration. Dr. Bruce has not reported on the medical service at the front; a defence of that service brought into ia discussion of Dr. Bruce's report is, if it was intentional, made for the purpose of drawing attention from the matter under discussion. The situation in not improved by the known facts of tli*
397G

case as set out in cold type in the reports that have been placed om the Table. After two years of war, the then Minister of Militia, on the evidence gathered by him by personal observation, came to the conclusion that a reorganization or improvement of the medical service in England was necessary or advisable. He selected, for the purpose of making inquiry, and for the purpose of reorganizing that medical service if inquiry should develop that it needed reorganization, one of the most eminent surgeons in Canada. Evidently, whatever other mistakes the then Minister of Militia may have made, he made no mistake in that appointment. The report of Dr. Bruce, dated September 20, is a most complete review of the medical or the hospital situation in the British Isles so far as it concerns the Canadian forces. It is evidently undertaken by a man who has the confidence of experience and reputation. He sets out in good plain English the conditions as he finds them and makes specific recommendations for the improvement of those conditions. Did the Government act on that report? They did not. As soon as the report was made public, there was a noise throughout England, from one end of the country to the other. Bruce's report was discussed in the English papers. What was the trouble with Bruce's report? In some portion of his report he had declared that it was more advisable that Canadian wounded should be cared for in Canadian hospitals by Canadian surgeons and physicians than that they should be scattered indiscriminately throughout the hospitals in the British Islands. Because he reported that, his report was criticised from one end of England to the other. For what reason? On the question of the medical treatment received by the Canadians? Not at all; but on the question .whether it was desirable or not to educate them in Imperialism, if you please, by spreading them around amongst their Imperial fellow-soldiers.
Have you any objection to that?
Did ray hon. friend say that the Prime Minister stated he did not want this done because it might injure recruiting?
I understood that.
He .said it would not be wise to have too much said about the facts.
He said it was contrary to the national interest.
He said it was contrary to the national interest that confidential information contained in the report should be made public.
It might give information to the enemy.

We shall have to say this, that so far as the Government are concerned in connection with this report, they certainly have been careful to give information neither to friends nor to enemies. This report, which was published in England as soon as it was made, which was printed in England for public distribution, which was published in the newspapers in England and spread from end to end of the United Kingdom within .a day or two .after it appeared, has never yet been printed in Canada fox the information of the people of this country, and even the English reprint that is here would never have been laid on the table of the House had a demand not been made on the Government for that measure of publicity. Yet, that being the case, when the question is raised again, and Dr. Bruce's reply to the B.abtie investigation is asked for by this House, we .axe told in effect that the Government have this report in their hands -and they will make it .public ox not as they .please.
Dr. Bruce is .at the present time in the British service. He .is not in civilian life. He is in a position in which ihe may be condemned to the limit and he has not the .privilege of reply. The .abuse of the power of the Government to prevent Dr. Bruce from making a public statement in justification of hi.s own position cannot have my support. As a member of this House of Commons, this free Parliament of the people of Canada, speaking for the people who are interested in this matter even more than Dr. Brace or the Government is, I for one demand the publication of Dr. Brace's statement .at the earliest possible date, and if it is not published I will hold the Government .as condemned, as not daring to publish t'he truth, as unwilling to justify or permit to be justified one of the Canadians who have .suffered and are .suffering in this war, and whose service has been a credit to Canada, as it is to-day admitted to be a benefit to the British military service.

In view of the .minister's statement that he .received a cablegram from Dr. Brace asking him for the publication of the report, does the minister intend to comply with the request of Dr. Bruce or not? I take it that the minister has a copy of the report in his possession.

My hon. friend was in the House when the Prime Minister made his very full statement. He stated that he intended to cable Sir George Perley in regard to the matter. I asked him whether he intended to cable himself or whether I should, and he said that he would cable. He stated over and over again that he did not want to lay the report on the Table until he had heard from Sir George Perley. That is what I understood him to say; I do not know whether my hon. friend understood him differently.

What the Prime
Minister said was this. He read the statement he made on the 31st of May, when we asked him to bring down the report, in which he said he was sending it to Sir George Perley for his examination. Dr. Bruce communicated ten days ago with the Minister of Militia to vhom he had sent the report; the report was not sent to Parliament. What answer did my hon. friend make to Dr. Bruce's cable?
I did not reply to it, .as it called for no reply.

Does the minister
say that at no time since the 31st of May has he had any communicatjon with Sir George Perley as to whether he received the repeat, and what he had to say about it?

The report was
sent to Sir George Perley, as stated by the Prime Minister.
Did he acknowledge receipt of it?

He has it in his
possession.
' Mr. MACDONALD: The facts, then, are these. My hon. friend has a copy of Dr. Bruce's report, and Sir George Perley has a copy, but Sir GeoTge Perley has not communicated his views on the report to the minister. Why, therefore, does not the minister lay on the Table the report which he has in his possession?

Because I am not going to override the Prime Minister's wishes. I am subject to the Prime Min-

ister; he is not subject to me. He has stated what he intends to do about it, and I am not going to do anything different.

Then there is this
confusion between my hon. friend and his leader. His leader stated that he was going to cable Sir George Perley to find out whether he had received the report. My hon. friend says that he knows Sir George Perley has had the report for some time, and has taken no exception to it. There is therefore no reason why the report should not be published. The minister's explanation of the situation is quite different from the Prime Minister's.
There is no difference so far as I can see.

The Prime Minister
thought the report might have been sunk.

My hon. friend the Minister of Militia is in a position at all events to relieve the mind of the Prime Minister as to the fate of the report, because as the hon. member for South Renfrew remarked the Prime Minister expressed some fear that it might have gone down in a ship that had been torpedoed. The Minister of Militia is able to reassure the Prime Minister that that fate did not befall the report but that it is now in the hands of his colleague the Overseas Minister of Militia. The Minister of Militia here has also a copy of it. This discussion as it proceeds becomes increasingly valuable, because almost every other minute it elicits a new admission-an admission which the time of the committee should not have been taken up in eliciting at all. Why all this mystery, all this desire for rfelay in this connection? Why is it that this committee and this House and this Parliament are treated in this way? As I recall the statement made by the Minister of Militia, who, I must say, is usually very, very frank indeed with the committee and with the House, he stated first of all that he had not received the original report. He was questioned! several times about the Bruce report and eaid that it had not reached him. Then he admitted receiving some mysterious letter from an unnamed place from some one.
I have all the letters in my possession, too.
He kept up the mystery in that way-
Who kept up the mystery? I did not.
The mystery was kept up. My hon. friend has been very unfortunate in the mails. Some perverse fate seems to be pursuing him in connection with this supplementary report.
Would my hon. friend be good enough to state plainly what he means. Does he mean to insinuate that I have given information to the House in connection with this matter which was not true?

I am not making any insinuations, but endeavouring to recall what the minister said. My memory may be at fault in some immaterial particulars. I was merely pointing out that from the inception of this discussion an atmosphere of fog has been thrown around this whole thing which the committee and the members of the Opposition have been unable to penetrate. I was pointing out that the Minister of Militia stated some months ago, when inquiry was made about this report, that it had not reached him, and he repeated that statement over and over again when questioned in the House. Then he admitted that he had received a letter later on, but that it was undated or unsigned or did not contain the sender's address.
That is absolutely correct.

And because of that he could not tell us about the report. I am only recalling these things to show what a long process was gone through before we finally nailed down somebody to something about this report. To-day, again, the same performance goes on, and the Overseas Minister of Militia is conveniently brought in at different stages. At one stage it is uncertain whether he received the report. At another, we are told that he has received it. The Prime Minister reads a statement he made in the House two months ago, when he said that he was going to communicate with the Overseas Minister of Militia. Two months have elapsed, and apparently he has not done that yet.
Remember, Dr. Bruce is naturally solicitous about his own reputation and anxious to have the veracity of his statements established. Dr. Bruce, it seems, has cabled the minister asking that the report be laid on the Table. That reminds me that my hon. friend was not just as candid as I gave him credit for a few moments ago, for he made that admission only upon being questioned from this side of the House. He

did not volunteer that statement; it was dragged out of 'him.

I answered the
question when it was asked. The information was not dragged out of me; I had quite forgotten about it.

So the standard set up
by my hon. friend the Minister of Militia is this. He, as Minister of Militia, as a servant of the people of this country, does not consider himself under any obligation to place the facts concerning any matter in his department before this committee, unless it should happen that some member on this side of the House has personal knowledge regarding it and asks the minister a question about it. I submit that this is a most improper position for a minister to take. He should give the committee all the information at his disposal, and so save the time of the committee and the time of the House.
What was the position assumed by the Prime Minister? The Prime Minister must have been in possession of the information that is in the possession of the Minister of Militia. The Minister of Militia says that a copy of this report is in the hands of the Overseas Minister of Militia. The Prime Minister gets up and professes not to have any knowledge of that, and intimates as a reason for not having any knowledge of it that the report may have gone down in some ship that was torpedoed. He was going to cable to-day to ascertain what the man sitting in the next chair to him knew, and could have told him if he had only turned in his direction. I submit that that is not treating this committee and this House and this country properly. This is too serious a matter to be trifled with in this way. "Trifled" is the only parliamentary term that I am permitted to apply to it, but I would apply a much stronger term if the rules of the House permitted me to do so.
My hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) has properly drawn the attention of the committee and of the Government to the responsibility of the Government in this matter. That responsibility is so grave, and this is a matter that comes so intimately home to so many people in this country, that I submit to the Minister of Militia that in justice to himself, in justice to the Government of which he is a member, in justice to the committee and to the House of Commons and the people of this country, and quite irrespective of what his leader has said, it i6 his duty to see that the cable
is sent to Sir George Perley this evening and that no more delay takes place.
I submit we should have this matter cleared up by to-morrow at the very latest and that this committee should not sit from day h>
day, passing the estimates of my hon. friend while this air of mystery surrounds such an important question. A cablegram from Sir George Perley will let us know what his position is, and what objection he has, if any, to the production of this report. Candidly 1 am sick and tired of this fable which is spun from the other side of the House to the effect that this, that, and the other'thing cannot be produced because it may give information to the enemy. To use a vernacular expression, that should be about played out. My hon. friend will remember that I made a motion for the production of a mobilization scheme of the Canadian forces which I understand was drawn up in 1913. This was a scheme with which everybody in and around Ottawa was perfectly familiar and which was a matter of common gossip. Instead of being carried out it was ignored, and this Government by reason of ignoring it has lost for the country tens of millions of dollars. I asked for the production of a copy of that mobilization scheme and the minister requested that the matter should not be pressed, that it was undesirable in the public interest that the documents should be produced. This scheme was four years old, yet it was supposed it might give information to the enemy. I recall this only to show my hon. friend the Minister of Militia that he is the victim of a system, and for the sake of his own good reputation and the honour and benefit of the country that system should be got rid of as quickly as possible. He can make a beginning in that direction by seeing that a cable is sent to Sir George Perley this evening, so that we may have a reply by to-morrow at the latest, and may know exactly where we stand with regard to this supplementary report of Dr. Bruce. I may remind my hon. friend that his ex-colleague asked a very pointed question about this matter, and received very little satisfaction. From the question I should infer that the contents of this mysterious report are not, after all, so mysterious or so hard to get at as my right hon. friend the Prime Minister and my hon. friend the Minister of Militia would have this committee believe. I again press upon the minister the absolute necessity, in the public interest as well as in his own interest, of having a cablegram sent tonight.	.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

After Recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

Motion agreed to.
Bill reported and read the third time and passed.
The House resumed in 'Committee of Supply, M.r. Rainville in the Chair.

While greater attention has been paid to that portion of Dr. Bruce's report which deals with the distribution of the Canadian wounded in hospitals in Great Britain, really the most important feature of his report and the one upon which he lays the greatest stress is the condition that results in the landing and maintaining in England of large numbers of men unfit for service at the front. It is with this point that Dr. Bruce deals most fully in his report on that question. He shows there is a condition in England that is detrimental to the efficiency of the military forces of Can-

ad'a and is seriously burdensome upon the treasury of Canada without any resulting benefit. In fact the result, as cducumistances are now, is a double loss, because the men who are not of military value in England would be of industrial value in Canada, and Canada is deprived of their services in industrial life, while we are receiving no benefit from them in military service. That at least is the evidence of Dr. Bruce, Dr. Jones and Dr. Babtie.
It is necessary that the people of Canada should understand to what extent this condition has prevailed and what it means to the people of Canada that it does prevail, and who is responsible for its existence. Seme weeks ago the member for Parry Sound (Mr. Arthurs) stated from his place in the House that there were 12,900 medically unfit men in service in England, and he recommended, very properly, that these men be brought back to Canada for industrial employment. I have asked for a statement of the number of medically unfit men who have been brought back to Canada.

I am not sure
whether those statistics have been given to the House. A great number of statistics have been furnished. All of those statistics which will be available are now available, and if these figures have not been given and if we have them I shall bring them down.

These figures were not contained in the statement made by the minister on a previous occasion. I have, however, a statement on that point that I shall take the liberty of placing before the House, and that is sufficiently startling. I have here a statement in regard to sixteen battalions going overseas during 1916. They are as follows: The 96th, Saskatchewan; the 111th, London, Ontario; the 113th, Lethbridge, Alberta; the 130th, Perth, Ontario; the 136th, Port Hope, Ontario; the 140th, St. John, New Brunswick; the 145th, St. John, New Brunswick; the 146th, Kingston, Ontario; the 151st, Edmonton, Alberta; the 152nd, Weyburn, Saskatchewan; the 179th, Winnipeg, Manitoba; the 189th, Fraserville, Quebec; the 142nd, London, Ontario; the 160th, Walkerton, Ontario; the 161st, Clinton, Ontario; the 168th, Woodstock, Ontario. Of these battalions, the 96th arrived in England with a strength of 770. Of these 111 were unfit for service, being a percentage of 14.43. The strength of the 111th of London, Ontario, was 635; the number

unfit for service was 185, the percentage of unfits being 29.13.

Does my hon. friend mean unfit for active military service at the front?
Mr. OLIVER. Yes.

Or entirely unfit? Some men are passed as unfit for service in France, or at the front, but are still retained in the reserve battalions. Does my hon. friend mean that these men are relegated back to civil life, out of the service entirely, or has he figured on that?
I have been asking the minister for these figures. I am giving the figures of the men listed as unfit for service at the front, the men who will never go to France.

Not necessarily. They may not at the moment be fit for service. They may not be ready to be classed in Category A, but they may be fit for service after a while. There are several categories in the table which I presented. It does not follow that alj these men are not fit for service ultimately.

I do not know that they
will all be unfit finally, but they were unfit o;n their 'arrival in England, and I will give some further facts as to why they were unfit, which will show they will never go to France. This may not apply to all, but it will apply to a large proportion. I want to know what is the policy of the Government in regard to these men who can never go to France. The 113th Battalion, Lethbridge, Alberta, had 879 men, 153 unfit for service, percentage 17.14. The 130th of Perth, Ontario, 554 men, 64 unfit, percentage 11.55. The 136th of PoTt Hope, Ontario, 472 men-less than 500 when they arrived in England-and of that number 144 were unfit for service, 30.50 per cent. The 140th of St. John, New Brunswick, 822 men, of whom 18 were unfit for service, 2.19 per cent. The 145th of St. John, N.B. 524 men, 82 unfit, 15.66 per cent. The 146th of Kingston, Ontario, arrived in England with 576 men, of whom 72 were unfit for service, 12.2 per cent. The 151st of Edmonton, Alberta, arrived in England with 907 men, 136 unfit for service,-14.99 per cent. The 152nd of Weyburn, Saskatchewan, 742 men, 187 unfit, 25.20 per cent. The 179th of Winnipeg, Manitoba, had 890 men, 116 were unfit, 13.03 per cent. The 189th of Fraserville, Quebec, 561 men, 99 unfit, 17.64 per cent. The 142nd of London, 561 men, 164 unfit, 29 peT cent.
The 160th of Walkerton, 997 men, 140 unfit, 13 per cent. The 161st of Clinton, Ontario, 740 men, 67 unfit, 9 per cent. The 168th of Woodstock, Ontario, 604 men, 87 unfit, 13 per cent. The average percentage of men unfit for service in this list of sixteen battalions was sixteen. There was sixteen per cent of the men who arrived overseas unfit for service in France.
Are those figures oflicial, from the department, or what is the source of that information?
I am giving these figures on the best information I have.
What is the information?

It would not be of any value to the hon. gentleman to give the source of information. I am giving the House the best information I have on the subject, and it will be for the department to show these figures not correct, if thiaf is the fact.	.
That is hardly reasonable.
That is the best I can do at the present time, but I am satisfied it will be found the figures are correct.
When were these men declared unfit? Immediately on landing, or some time after?

I presume as soon after landing as .a medical examination is ordinarily held. The statement I have is that the men, on landing in England, were medically unfit for service in France. They were perfectly healthy men and good for civil life, but the .point I desire to make is in the case of these sixteen battalions, sixteen per cent of the men sent over to England were of no military value to us, while they would have been of industrial value had they remained at home, and I am anxious to know if the department intends to bring them back, or what is its policy in regard to these men, and how many of theim are there?
I want to say, on what I believe is good, sound and reliable information, that I do not think the hon. gentleman's figures are correct, in regard to the 146th.
Perhaps I can give tlhe explanation. I take it from the numbers of these battalions that they went last fall.
Some time during 1916.

Last fall the 'authorities in France made a new rule, excluding 'ail over 40 years of age, and all under 20, from service in France during the winter. I think the hon. gentleman will find that these two arbitrary exclusions, applying only to the severe weather of the winter, account far nearly 'all these unfits of whom he has been reading to the House.

Whatever reason there was for their unfitness, the point is that these men were enlisted for military service in France. The man who is not in a condition to perform military service in France has no right to be enlisted.

Does my hon. friend take into account the number of men who took sick on the overseas journey and were quarantined upon their arrival? In the 168th Battalion, with which the member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) is quite familiar, a considerable number of men were quarantined immediately upon their arrival in England.
They were not sent back.
Sixteen battalions, comprising 11,234 men, arrived in England, and of that number of men 1,825 were medically unfit, an average of 16 per cent.
Not medically unfit.

I mean unfit for service in France. I have here the causes of unfitness in regard to twelve of these battalions. In these twelve battalions 1,367 men were listed as unfit for service in France. The cause of disability were as follows: under age 515, over age, 334.
That bears out the statement of my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor).
To some extent. Of course, those who are over age will never be fit for service; those who are under age will become fit in time.
Those who are over age are fit now, because in the summer they take men up to 45, whereas in the severe winter they exclude those who are over 40.
Does my hon. friend say that they bring back from France in the winter the men who are over 40 years of age?
No, they do not send them to France when they are over 40. They send them when the fine weather comes.
What do they do with them when the winter comes round?
-Unfortunately, very few men last that long. It is- a very lucky battalion whose men, sent out in the spring, are still serving the next winter.
Many of them have been there two years.
The casualties, for instance, in the 7th Battalion from British Columbia in the first year of its service were 1,500, the total strength of the battalion being 1,100.

That is hardly the point. I understood the hon. gentleman to say that my figures were misleading, because men were not allowed to go to France during the winter, because of their being over age, would be allowed to go in the summer. If they went in the summer, what happened to them when the winter came around? My hon. friend says that they would, all be killed by that time.

A large proportion of
them would be invalided, either killed or wounded.

Suppose they did not
happen to be invalided?

Those who were not invalided would be kept in France. This age limit of 40 is quite new; it was introduced only last December. When these men were enlisted in Canada, 45 was the age limit, whether for service in France, England or Canada. But the experience in France showed that men of that age were not able to stand the severe weather in the trenches; therefore last December an order was made to send forward to France no more men over 40 during tha winter months.
The only difficulty about my hon. friend's explanation is that the date of the information that I have here is October 27.

I hope the hon. gentleman does not want to hold me to a day. I say December, because I was there in December. It is possible that the order was issued shortly before I got there; I know that it was very new when- I got there.

My information is dated
October 27, and it relates to those battalions which had been going over some time during the summer. Certainly, there fore, that was previous to the special rule which my hon. friend mentions.
An hon. gentleman reminds me that it -was early in November that we reached England, not December, as I stated.

In any case the date of
these figures is certainly previous to the rule my hon. friend has mentioned.

Suppose it was, would
these men not be kept a certain length of time in England in order to complete their training? That would run them well into December or January, when they would be singled out in accordance with the method set forth by the member for New Westminster (Mr. Taylor).

The state of facts that I
am placing before the committee existed before the date my hon. friend speaks of as the time of the introduction of this new Tule.

I think the hon. gentleman is wrong about his dates, because the numbers of the battalions that he refers to indicate that those battalions were in summer camps last summer. My battalion, for instance, was the 131st; it was not unduly delayed in Canada. Most of these numbers are higher than 131.

I am afraid that the position will have to stand as I have stated it. My information, bearing date the 27th October, relates to the arrival in England of battalions before that date and to the conditions which existed in regard to these battalions at the time they were reported upon. Let me give the figures, then:	Of these 1,367 men out
of twelve battalions, 515 were under age 334 were over age. There were 200 with flat and defective feet, 63 wilth defective vision, 27 with varicose veins, 15 with defective legs, 13 were immature, 13 lhad defective iheart, and 187 bad miscellaneous defects. As to those who were over .age, or who were otherwise permanently physically defective, the department will have to (answer to the people of Canada for having taken them over to England when they did not intend to use them in France. They must answer also, for keeping them in England instead of returning them to industrial employment in Canada. That is the point I wish to make, and that is why I have asked the Government so frequently for the figures in regard to this matter, which is a very serious one. Very few people in Canada thought that, as the member for Parry Sound (Mr. Arthurs) started, 'there were
12,900 of these men in England who could not be of military value to our country. If there were 12,900 there .at that time I w.ant to know how many have already been returned to Canada, because I can hardly imagine that the department has not from time to time returned some of these men to this country. A burden has been placed upon the resources of 'Canada by putting these men in military service for which they were not fitted, and the industries of Canada have been hampered by reason of these men being taken out of industrial life. That is not management of which this country has any right to be proud, or upon which the Government can .plume itself as having taken reasonable measures to win the war.
The hon. gentleman, I assume, will admit that all these men were medically examined before they left Canada by competent medical practitioners.

Oh, no. I have the Babtie report on that point. I have already placed it before the House, but seeing that my hon. friend raises the question, I may as well let him know what Dr. Babtie has to say about it. Dr. Babtie says:
The Board is satisfied that there have been large numbers of men passed who ought not to have been passed by the (medical officer; but it was perhaps inevitable under the circumstances of raising the Canadian Expeditionary Force that examinations could not be conducted with all the care necessary. This it believes to have been due partly to inexperience on the part of the examining medical officer, partly to hurry, partly to carelessness, and lastly, in some instances, to the opinion of an examining medical officer being overridden or ignored by commanding officers.
This report is dated 22nd December, 1916. Dr. Babtie goes on to say:
These defects in recruiting continue to exist despite medical examinations by recruiting medical officers, by battalion medical officers of adjoining units and before sailing for the United Kingdom.

Does the hon. gentleman suggest any way in which the Government could have done better than they did in appointing reputable medical men throughout the whole country for the purpose of examining soldiers?

The conclusion of the
Babtie commission is that they did not.
-Mr. MORPHY: What is your conclusion?

This is what Dr. Babtie
says.
My hon. friend should not say that. He did not read that.
The medical examiner who is careless in his report is surely not a reputable examiner.
The best medical man might sometimes be careless.
He cannot maintain his reputation on actions of carelessness.
The Government cannot supervise each man's work.
But Dr. Babtie uses the expression that this condition is partly due to inexperience.

Inexperience in examina

tions for purposes of war.
That is to say, the Government are appointing inexperienced examiners.
At the beginning of the war there was no medical officer experienced in examining troops for overseas.
How much experience had Dr. Bruce along that line?

Thjs is not Dr. Bruce's opinion. I am giving Dr. Babtie's opinion; but Dr. Babtie, Dr. Bruce and Dr. Jones all agree specifically that this condition has existed in Canada; that it exists without excuse, and that it is a great and unjustifiable burden upon the people of Canada and militates against the military efficiency of our forces overseas. That is the position.
Can the hon. member give me the figures for the 110th Battalion?
I have not the figures for the 110th Battalion; I have the figures for the 111th.
Where is the 111th Battalion from?
London, Ontario.
I do not think the information the hon. member has is accurate.

Either the information that I hold in my hands is cprrect, or it is incorrect. The Militia Department have the information that I profess to be giving to the House, and they can verify it or contradict it at their convenience. As a matter of fact, there is no doubt that the information is correct.

Last fall orders were
given that before any troops should pro-

ceed overseas, the medical officer of the battalion had to pass on every man that that man was medically fit for overseas. I know of four battalions. After they arrived in England, they had a great deal of sickness-spinal meningitis, measles and so on. Each week the medical officer of the battalion had to send in a report of the number of men who were fit, and all those men who were quarantined were put down as unfit to go to France. Perhaps that may account for some of the large figures the hon. member has given.

I have given details of
the classes and none of them is in that class. They would be a different class altogether. These are the men who are permanently unfit; that is, they are men who should not have been enlisted and who should not have been passed after they were enlisted.

How did they get
past the board?

That is due to the inexperience of the board. If Dr. Babtie, Dr. Jones and Dr. Bruce do not agree upon anything else, they all agree upon that. It is not my argument or contention; I am giving the very best authority available on the subject. There is no doubt about the facts, and the facts are deplorable. As the matter has not been brought up, I think I can find in Dr. Bruce's report, a list
The hon. member said that several hundreds of those were turned down for being under age. He would not call such men permanently unfit.

Does varicocele make
a man permanently unfit?

He has varicocele, senility, too old. Another man has deformed legs. The disabilities of others are: dyspnoea, defective feet, index finger missing; middle finger, left hand deformed, varicocele ; deformed left hand, unable to flex fingers, unable to march; age, varicose veins; over age, rheumatism; age and debility; heavy weight, 215 pounds, with poor feet, unable to march; age and general physical condition; flat feet and fits; bad feet, sluggish mentality; age and debility; myalgia, subject to spells of dizziness; age and debility; chronic bronchitis, over age; age, general physical condition; mentally unfit; hernia, one leg one and one-half inches shorter than the other; varicocele interferes with marching, refuses operation; age and debility; large bunion, age; age and debility; age and debility; weak back; involuntary urination, dyspnoea; age and teeth; deafness and over age; height 4 feet 9 inches, weight 112 pounds, spinal caries; atrophied left arm, no development since nine years; amputated thumb of each hand; glass eye, 1 tooth upper jaw, 17 lower jaw, over age; severe varicocele, asthma, dyspnoea; aortic (regurgitation; deafness both ears.
I am not a medical man, but I think the medical men who are in the House will agree that there could not have been efficient medical examinations, or the men who are in these conditions could not and would not have been enlisted.
So the case is absolutely proven that the Department of Militia in raising these battalions did not employ, as they should have done competent and reliable medical officers. As a result the country hais been saddled with an enormous cost, and the efficiency of our troops at the front has been correspondingly reduced, while the industrial condition of the country has been placed at a disadvantage.
These mien my hon. friend has referred to were members of pioneer battalions.

I think my hon. friend
is wrong, hut I do not see that it makes any difference. Some oif these men were of the 52nd, 40th, 44th, 2nd and 1st Pioneer Battalions. If they were not fit for service at the front, it does not matter what kind of a battalion they were enlisted in; we had no business to enlist them, and the Government is responsible for enlisting and having kept them.

My hon. friend will notice that on page 95 of the Report it says:
I am enclosing herewith a nominal roll of a few cases which have passed through this office, and would call your special attention to the enclosed roll of one unit, namely, the 2nd Pioneer Battalion, from which some thirty-eight or foity men alone were discharged under A.F.B. 204 as useless from physical defects.

I do not catch the purpose of my hon. friend in drawing attention to the fact that these are pioneer battalions. If so many very, veTy bad cases were found in one battalion, surely it is proven beyond all argument that the medical officer examining for that battalion was certainly not efficient. One occasional case may get by, but with a list like that, there is no question that the examining officer did not do his duty.
The medical examination *for a pioneer battalion is not so strict as for other battalions.

These men were not accepted Wihen they got to England, but were culled out, and very properly so. I wish to draw attention to another matter in this connection. Of the sixteen battalions in the list I have here which were sent over to England, one was a little over 500 strong, and five were under 600 strong. None of them were at full strength. As a matter of fact, we sent sixteen battalion establishments across the water when we only had men enough, after the culls were taken out, for eight 'battalions; that is, we sent over a double supply of officers for the number of men we sent over.
What authority has my hon. friend for saying that we sent over a full quota of officers in battalions that were not at full strength?
Does my hon. friend say that he did not?
I am asking my hon. friend a question.

My full belief is that he did send over a full quota of officers in eacti
case.
Only in proportion to the number of the rank and file.
My hon. friend is Minister of Militia, and knows what he has done and what he has not done.
That is absolutely right.

I have some personal acquaintance with one of these battalions.

I see that it is under strength, and I know that it went over with a full quota of officers. I do not know why that battalion should be treated cfifferently from any other battalion.

Which battalion was it?
. Mr. OLIVER: The 151st. I will admit tnat it is the nearest to full strength of any battalion in the list, with 907 men. A battalion, I think, is something over 1,100 men.
lit is 1,035, including officers.

I have no reason to suppose that this battalion was treated differently from any other battalion, or to think that when the full allowance of officers went over with that battalion, a full allowance of officers did not go over with the other battalions.
Not at all.
I suppose my hon. friend will admit that a lieutenant-colonel went over with each battalion?
Very likely.

The principal officer went over, and those next in command, I suppose? The position is this: We sent over men enough for eight or nine battalions, and we sent over officers out of proportion to the number of men. That will have to be admitted, because we sent over 16 lieutenant-colonels when we only had men enough for eight or nine battalions. We knew before those battalions sailed from Canada that there was no position on the other side of the water for some of these 'colonels, but yet we sent them over and I am afraid we are keeping them over there. Now that is a condition for which there is certainly no excuse, and it does not tend to efficiency or satisfaction. When we were discussing this matter in the House before, some hon. gentlemen said:	"If reinforcements are wanted in France, you must take the men and leave the officers." Very true, but we have a military organization- and a military administration in Canada, and when we deliberately authorize the raising of battalions over and above our possibilities, we are responsible for having given that authorization, and responsible for the consequences of it; and when we were sending these battalions over under strength, if we had dealt honestly and fairly with these battalion officers we should have said to them before they went over: "You have not raised a full battalion, and therefore you cannot go to England." It would

have been a more decent thing to do to stop them on this side of the water, rather than to send the battalions over with a full quota of officers, and then turn the officers adrift or keep them on the paylist without duties to perform. Such a condition of affairs could only result as it has resulted, in spreading dissatisfaction with military service throughout the country. In the first year of the war we had a large measure of military enthusiasm, which would have responded to the full to any reasonable call that might have been made upon it, but the administration of our military forces has been such that the enthusiasm has been killed, and then the Government comes to us and says: "The patriotism of our people has declined and we must now resort to compulsory military service." The position is absolutely unfair; it is unjust; it is an attempt by the Government of the day to protect the mismanagement of our military forces by discrediting the patriotism of our people.

The question my hon. friend referred to in the latter part of his remarks is one which has been discussed on more than one occasion during this session of the House. There were quite a number of battalions sent over which were not up to full strength. The number of officers sent with those regiments was in proportion to the number of the rank and file, and the commanding officer was left to choose the officers he should take with him. The commanding officer knew before be left Canada that he was going over in command of a battalion and that he would not likely be able to go to the front* but that he would be returned to Canada. His officers also knew this. The junior officers had the privilege, of course, of reverting to a lower rank. The situation was not one for which the Government was responsible. Recruiting dropped off and those battalions could not be filled up, and there did not seem to be any prospect of them being filled up, so it was thought better to send them over as they were. In view of all that has been said on this point, I do not think it necessary to go any further with it, beyond stating that the situation was well understood. Tire officers in command of those partly completed battalions knew all the circumstances before they went over. At the same time, I have always contended it would not have been fair to those officers to have robbed them of even their commands by preventing them from taking their battal-

ions overseas as they stood. Some of those officers performed very good service when they reached the other side; others have come back to Canada, and some have gone hack into civil life.
How many such officers have returned to Canada, say in [DOT]the last year?

I could not give the exact figure, but the number was fairly large. Every day there are men reverting to civil life, because there is nothing further for them to do. I have letters from many of them stating they are perfectly satisfied. They have done all they could, and it was not their fault that they could not get to the front, or that they could not recruit their battalions to full strength. This is a situation which has come about quite naturally and for which no one is to blame. Every one did the best he could to get those battalions up to strength.
My hon. friend has also referred to a number of battalions for which he has statistics. I do not know where those returns came from, and I do- not know on what they are based, or who is responsible for them. However, taking the returns asi he gives them to the House, I understand thirteen per cent of the whole number were thought to be unfit for service when they reached England.
Sixteen per cent.

If my hon. friend had said twenty-five par cent were unfit for service at the front I would have felt it was a very good showing indeed. Those men arrived after the hardships.of a sea voyage; many of them in a condition very different *from their condition when, they sailed. Besides that, as my hon. friend has pointed out, a large proportion of them were under age. Now, what does "under age " mean? Under the voluntary system imen have been taken from 18 to 45 years of age. Within the last two years, I think, it has been decided that no man shall go- to the front unless he is at least 19 years of
9 p.m. >age. So those men who enlisted here in good faith at 18 years of age and went across would not be able to go to France until they were 19. Men of 45 were unable to get to the front, because they could not -stand the climate. Tlhese two reasons account for the majority of those who were not fit to go to France at once. Apart from that, o<ur men are not fit to go into the trenches immediately they reach England, because they
have to receive considerable intensive training and preparation before they are fit for the firing line. As has already been pointed out, they are divided into categories, A, B, C, D land E. There are five classifications under category A; there -are -three iclassifioa-ti-ons under category B, -and there are three classifications under category 0. All those men were made use of. If a man in England, although not fit for the -trenches, is cap-able of performing some other duty, -it is just as difficult to arrange to get him home as it is to get -a mian out of the trenches. There are iall sorts of duties to be performed on lines -of communication, clerical duties, base duties, preparing camp, land so on. I need not weary the House with a summary of the strength of -all the units of the C. E. F. in England on the 14th of M-ay, 1917. This statement was laid on the table during the time the Military Service Bill wias under consideration. There were 126,241 men in England at that time; 26,359 of those men were in category Al, fit for the trenches. The others were undergoing training and were in different categories, preparing for the higher category. In order to understand how these imen are qualified, and what is done -with them in England, I should have to weary the committee with facts and figures, and I do not wish to do it to-night. This material has -already been placed on Han-s-ard. It is a l-ong document, showing the subdivision in each category, and why the men are not fit -for the trenches immediately they arrive in England. I have the -docu-m-ent before me, land I could have copies of it prepared -and furnished to any member of the committee who may desire the information. These imen were enlisted in Cahiada in good faith. Of course, -there wiere some oases -of -men -slipping -through the doctors' hands, as was explained this afternoon, without having passed a proper medical examination. My *hon. friend referred to. the men with flat feet. There has been more attention paid to that of late. It is pretended those men cannot march as well as the others, but, in every other way they are just as fit for the trenches. The examination i-n this regard has been -made more rigid -lately. I read to the Bouse this -afternoon a statement showing that out of about 1,600 troops reaching England lately there were only five who were unfit for service, and I gave the reasons why those five were unfit. The statistics which my hon. friend read to -the House were in reference to a pioneer battalion. Medical examination for a pioneer battalion or ia forestry battalion is alto-



gother different from whia>t if) is for infantry, *artillery or cavalry.	_
These men do not undergo the same medical examination, but they are able, for the most part, to perform the duties for which they enlisted. The occurrence of these things in the early days of the war is no reflection upon the great bulk of the medical men. They were generally civilian doctors, unaccustomed to military regulations, and, of course, we were all new to the game.
