But the regulations have been strengthened and made more exacting, and, after we had a certain amount of experience, the results were very satisfactory.

This whole question would be very much more clear if the Government had been in a position to tell us whether they proposed to act upon the Babtie report or the Bruce report or the Jones report. They take the position of discrediting the Bruce report; they apparently do not intend to pay any attention to it and have taken the ground that Dr. Babtie's report completely answered everything contained in the Bruce report, and that there was nothing to be done. It will be remembered that in the Mesopotamia matter Dr. Carter, a medical man who stood in exactly the same position to Dr. Babtie as Dr. Bruce stands in regard to Dr. Babtie in the Canadian matter, was honoured by the British Government on account of having done very worthy service. The Government do not propose to have anything to do with Dr. Bruce's report. Let us look at some of the cases that are mentioned by Dr. Wilson, whose report is incorporated in that of Dr. Bruce:	Lt.-Col. Wilson
tells us of a man who went over there, Private Empson, who is 72 years of age? Is there any way under heaven by which a medical man, unless he was a political heeler, as they have been in many places, would pass men of 72 years of age? Then it is to be found at the same page of the report, page 97, that Private Alwright was taken out of a tuberculosis sanatorium previous to embarkation. On what principle would there be any justification for taking a man out of a tuberculosis sanatorium and sending him across to fight?
Who did it?

It will be found at page 97 of the report of Dr. Wilson. Private C. H. Baird was blind in the left eye and seven-eighths blind in the other eye, so that he was fifteen-sixteenths blind. Under what possible organization could such men as these be permitted to go to the other side on any service 
whatever? On page 94 we find the case of a young man, 16 years of age, who weighed 80 pounds. He had infantile paralysis, which left him with weak and undeveloped muscles in the right hip and thigh. He was passed by a doctor in Pembroke, and again examined at Quebec and passed by another doctor. He has done no military duty since he went over.
Was he in a pioneer or an infantry battalion?
He was in the 224th.
A pioneer battalion.

That makes no difference. What is the use of sending men 72 years of age, and blind, and men out of tuberculosis sanatoria, and with weak and undeveloped muscles? Then we find the cases of Private Dickson, 67 years of age; Private Jarvis, 52 years of age; Private Macdonald, 52 years of age, and Private Lockie, 52 years of age. These men were of no use over there. These statements are made upon the authority of men who, in regard to this medical service, so far as Canada is concerned, were doing exactly what Dr. Carter did with reference to Mesopotamia. The minister does not say he is doing anything in regard to all these reports about men who should never have gone and who have cost this country hundreds of thousands of dollars. On the contrary, the position of the Government is to discredit Dr. Bruce and his inquiry. The Prime Minister told us he would not bring down Dr. Bruce's report; he wanted to send it over to Sir George Perley because possibly there might be something in it which Sir George might want to answer. He sent it over some months ago, and Sir George Perley has it. The Minister of Militia has a copy of it, but will not show it to the House or to the country, and the consequence will be, if the Government maintain that position, that the session will close and the country will not have that report. That is apparently what the Government intend to do. The Government have no right to get any estimates through this House when they refuse to produce that report. It is contrary to every principle of constitutional privilege and parliamentary practice that, in regard to such a vital question as this the Government should ask Supply without giving necessary information, or should put forward such a flimsy excuse as they have done. What is there about Sir George Perley, who is he anyway,

that he should be the one man upon whose bidding the Parliament of Canada should wait for two months in order to find out whether he has something to say in regard to this matter? Is he any greater man than Dr. Babtie or Dr. Jones, both of whom made their answers in proper time? The first report of Dr. Bruce was made to the Minister of Militia here and was submitted to Parliament in due course. So was the report of Dr. Jones. So was the Babtie report. And when Dr. Brace deals with these important matters which we have been discussing and the remedying of which is in the interest of the prosecution of the war and of the country, he sends the report to the minister here, but it is not submitted to Parliament, and the excuse of the Prime Minister is:	I wanted to send it to Sir
George Perley, and I did so, and he has got it; we cannot tell whether we are going to bring it down or not. Is Sir George Perley greater than this Parliament or than the Canadian people? He has grown very big since he left this country. He did not seem to be possessed of such wonderful qualities when he was in Parliament with the rest of us. When did he become such a great military genius, and when was he endowed with such superlative qualities that Parliament must wait upon his pleasure? The position of the Government, in view of the facts given to the House and the country by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), in venturing to ask for Supply without giving that report, is one of the greatest pieces of effrontery we have ever had in this Parliament. The Government evidently do not intend to bring down the report and the session will probably close, and no report will be brought down.

It seems to me, following the line of discussion of the hon. gentleman from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), and my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), that there is some very distinct and. strong reason why the Government refuses to lay on the table of the House the second report of Dr. Bruce. The hon. Minister of Militia knows what that report contains. I do not know what it contains as a matter of positive knowledge, but I have some inkling of its contents. It probably contains a condemnation of Sir George Perley, by reason of his interference in regard to Dr. Bruce's Teport. I think it also condemns this Government very severely for the very thing the hon. gentleman from Edmonton has brought to the notice of this House to-night,
253)
namely the examination of the men before they left Canada. Hundreds of thousands of dollars have been lost to Canada, and the pension list has been enormously swollen, by reason of the very inaccurate, unwise-and careless examination of recruits before1 they left this country for England. I quite agree with the statement of the hon. gentleman from Pictou that the Minister of Militia should not be allowed any Supply until that report is laid on the Table and givien to the public of Canada. Dr. Bruce was an official of the Government. He was asked by the Minister of Militia to make a report, which he made. After that report was made, a second investigating committee was appointed in England to criticise that report, and they did criticize it, and Dr. Bruce has given his reply to that criticism. That reply, whatever it is, the people of Canada are entitled to have, and we should know its contents before money is voted for the carrying on of the affairs of the Militia Department. I feel just as strongly as the hon. gentleman from Pictou that the report must be given to the people of Canada before Supply is voted further for the militia services.

Mr. Chairman, during the transportation of the troops through the province of Quebec, especially by the Intercolonial, during the years 1915 and 1916, the soldiers who were being conveyed in the passenger trains have behaved in a manner not only obnoxious, but sometimes most scandalous.
I do not remember whether I wrote to the Militia Department about it, but, at any rate, I did report the case to the railway department in Moncton, and as member for the county, taking up the defence of [DOT] the citizens of my county, I have felt obliged to do it, for matters had become almost unbearable. I don't know where those chaps were coming from, for they seemed very little civilized, but all I do know is that they did mot speak French, and they must have come from the western provinces; that instead of conforming to the usages of civilized people, they behaved ruthlessly, neither more nor less. I will now read to the House a letter which I felt compelled to write to the general manager of the railway in Moncton, under date of August 21, 1916:
Sayabec, August 21, 1916.
J. K. McNeillie, Esq.,
Supt. Gen. C.G.R.,
Moncton, N.B.
Dear Sir,-
I write to inform you that every time I travel on the trains, since the soldiers are he-

ing transported, the passengers on our regular trains are constantly insulted hy those individuals who sing, yell, smoke, drink, vomit, and turn upside down everything in first and second class cars, to such an extent, that it is a disgrace for the .administration to tolerate such things.
We hear a great many people swearing against the. Conservative Government, for tolerating such conduct, and I think it is your duty to have this condition of things remedied at once. The employees are powerless.
We must prevent those individuals embarking on regular trains, or otherwise have a special car on each train, and further more have one or two policemen on train to keep them in good order. This state of things cannot be tolerated any longer, because it is prejudicial to the railroad which will lose passenger traffic, and also to our political prospects.
Those individuals insult men and children, and lay down in the alleys of the cars, and it is a dangerous matter to disturb them. X saw the porter on the car, at Valcartier, insulted, last night, in the most brutal manner, and I feel that those poor employees are not sufficiently protected against those brutes. A small number behave themselves properly, but the large number should not have access to those passenger cars.
Believe me, dear sir,
Tours faithfully,
H. Boulay.
It took about three weeks to get an answer to this letter, and finally the following reply, which was not very satisfactory, was received. I do not know which minister the manager refers to in his letter, whether it is the Minister of Militia or the Minister of Railways.
What is the date -of the letter?

September 8, 1916. It reads as follows:
Moncton, N.B., 8th September, 1916.
H. Boulay, Esq., M.P.,
Sayabec, Que.
Dear Sir,-
Referring to your letter of the 21st ultimo, matters of this kind must be referred to the minister so that I regret I can take no action.
Tours truly,
J. K. McNeillie. I
I do not think it was proper for the Department of Militia to. allow those men to travel on railroad trains in that condition, without having officers to look after them. Eor the last two years it has been a real disgrace, and, as a representative of a large county in the province of Quebec, through which those men are supposed to travel, I should not like those scenes to be repeated this year, and I urge strongly upon, the Department of Militia or the Department of Railways-I do not know which

has charge of such matters-to look after these men, and see that officers are put in charge of them, or that they be not allowed to travel on passenger trains. People complained several times to the superintendent, and they have complained to the general manager at Moncton, and I suppose they received a reply similar to this letter.
Mr. EDWARDS; Does the hon. member think they should he put on cattle trains?
They should be put on proper trains for soldiers, or, if put on passenger trains, there should be somebody to look after them.
Were these men from Valcartier camp?
I do not know where they were coming from, because they could not talk French.

Were they all brutes?
Mr. BOULAY7: They were acting like brutes.
I am very much surprised to hear a member of this House call the men who are going to the front to fight for us brutes.

From the way they were conducting themselves, no one could say anything else of them. I do not say they were all behaving that way; there were many real gentlemen among them, but too many of them could not behave themselves.

How did the conduct
of those soldiers to whom my hon. friend refers compare with the conduct of the Laval students, at the Montreal meeting, for instance?

We never have the Laval students on these trains; I cannot say how . they would behave.
(Translation): Mr. Chairman, I beg the House to .allow me to. add a few words as to- the organization of the battalions. There is some complaint that the province of Quebec did not enlist as largely as she ought to have done. I will point out that several reasons have prevented our soldiers from enlisting in larger numbers, and among these reasons I may mention, as one of the most important the breaking up of our battalions after they had gone across. I will cite as an example the case of the 189th of Rimouski and Temiscouata. This regiment had been recruited ~ by oompatent officers and under the formal promise that these officers would lead them oil the battlefield. I do not know what were the reasons,

but as soon as the battalion had reached England its officers were put aside and replaced by people who were perfect strangers to the soldiers of the 189th. The latter wrote home, informing their folks of what h.ad happened, and I am convinced that the disorganization of that battalion did largely contribute to prevent any further enlistment. I am prepared to *assert this .fact, for I ihave personally heard a large number of young men repeat that they would not enlist to submit to the fate of their comrades who had left with the 189th.
Now, I would like to have from the hon. Minister of Militia a declaration whether the regulations of the department permit the inflicting of punishments such .as those which are reported to have been, meted out to -the Canadian soldiers in England. It is reported, for instance, that soldiers have been forced to remain with their arms crossed for ten .or twelve consecutive hours.; another punishment which was inflicted, according to reports, is forcing men to run during the same length of time, with five minutes' rest at intervals, of fifteen or twenty minutes, and a 75^pound load on their shoulders. If military regulations contain such punishments nowadays, it seems to me that is a downright shame. I understand that such penalties can have been inflicted a hundred years ago.; but in our present state of civilization, men who are going to. risk -their lives on the battlefields should not be given such punishment. I would ask the hon. minister to tell me if such is actually the case; these reports circulate in my district, and, I repeat it, they are of such -a nature as to prevent many well-disposed young men from enlisting.

My hon. friend refers to the .punishment of soldiers in England for committing certain offences. Tlie punishment meted out to any soldier from Canada would be the same as the punishment meted out to any soldier who enlisted in Great Britain. I do- not know all the circumstances to which my hon. friend refers; there has been no complaint with regard to severe .punishment of our soldiers while in England or in France. There have been punishments, but there have been no complaints. I -cannot pass any judgment upon the matter to which my hon. friend refers unless I -have the particulars before me, or have an investigation made. My bon. friend refers also to the breaking up of the 189th Battalion. That was a very good battalion, indeed, but what
happened to 'it happened to battalions from all over Canada. You cannot keep a battalion intact very long. As was explained in the House to-night, some men drop off for various reasons -and are not fit to go to France. The moment the men go to France the wastage is very great and a unit has to be consolidated with reinforcements from other battalions. In the early stages of the war, when we saw a battalion going out of Canada we always felt that there was a battalion that was going right across the water to England and to France as .a unit. We did not understand then as well >as we do now the exigencies of war and the wastage which takes place in the battle line. Owing to these conditions, battalions from all over Canada have h.ad to be broken up; no condition existed with regard to the 189th that did not exist with regard to -all o'ther battalions.

Mr. -Chairman, I wish to. .say a few words about the. medical examination of our soldiers. I heard, a few minutes ago, some hon. members on the other side of the House criticising the Government for not having subjected our soldiers to a minute medical examination before sending them over to England, and I really believe that there has. been -some laxity in that regard. I will mention one case in order to show what were the shortcomings in this connection. Soldiers who had enlisted in the 150th, the 178th, and the 233rd, and who were being sent eastwards, met with a serious railroad -accident, their train leaving the track; some of them were killed outright and many others wounded. Some of these men, thirty-seven of them in all, were carried over to Partridge island, near Halifax, where they were examined three, weeks after their landing -and finally sent back home. I do not understand the reason of that trip in which the lives of these people were greatly exposed. These soldiers, were all of them French Canadians, and all of them told me they would have preferred being sent across the ocean, where they would .have been given the necessary care and could have later done their duty as well [DOT]as the other soldiers forming part of the regiment. Iif, on the other hand, thes-e men. were not fit to go and fight, it seems to .me they should have been spared the hardships of such a long voyage, and the country would .also have been saved the amount of their pay, of their allowances, and th.e other costs thereby incurred. I do hope that, as far as this' is concerned, the-Government have taken such measures that:
No. This happened every time I was on the train, and it also happened when I was not.

I am surprised
my hon. friend did not report the matter. He may have reported it before I was Minister of Militia, because he says that this occurred in September, 1916. His proper course, as a member of Parliament, would have been to report it to the Minister of Militia of that day. It is an improper thing for a soldier to conduct himself in any place in any other way than as a gentleman, and when soldiers do that sort of thing they are liable to be reprimanded by their superior officers, and they should be reprimanded. But I do not agree with the contention that soldiers should not travel on regular passenger trains. Our soldiers are citizens of Canada; they are on the same level as we are, and there is no reason for supposing that they will not conduct themselves in a proper manner. I have travelled on trains with soldiers in every part of this country, and I have never seen a soldier on a train conducting himself in any other way than that becoming a gentleman and soldier wearing the King's uniform.

I do not know if they
were conducting themselves in the wiay I have described intentionally in the province of Quebec, but if the minister asks for a report from every conductor who has taken soldiers on passenger trains, either the limited or the express, he will see that what I say is not exaggerated. We waited because we were always expecting that this abuse would cease. The trainmen reported the occurrence every time to their head officials, but they could never get satisfaction. It was only when we got sick of the whole matter that I decided to report it myself and I thought it was to the railway officials that I should report because they were closer to us than is the Minister of Militia.

I would like to ask
the minister as to the age limits of soldiers enlisting. Am I right in saying that 18 is the minimum and 41 the maximum age?
The age limits in Canada are from 18 to 45 under voluntary recruiting.
When a recruit offers to enlist does he have to make an affidavit as to his age?
He signs an attestation paper and swears to it.
I think it is a notorious fact that in the army there are many men under 18 or over 45. Do all these men sign an attestation paper?
Yes.

And are there no cases in which ambitious recruiting officers have winked at the attestation papers which were obviously signed by men outside the age limits? The reason I am calling the minister's attention to this matter is that one hears and reads of so many cases of this kind. I have here an item whifch appeared in the press in Montreal only a day or so ago:
Pte	 said to be the youngest soldier
who west to the front with any of the Canadian contingents, and probably one of the youngest soldiers of the Empire to go into the trenches, who has been missing since last Fall, is now
listed as presumed to be dead. Pte....
was only fourteen years of age. When he went to enlist, he gave his age as eighteen and was quickly accepted. He apparently fell in the battle of the Somme in which his battalion, a French Canadian regiment, was engaged. He has a brother in the army, who has been wounded.
:I cannot understand how a hoy of 14 could be accepted by a recruiting officer, even though he signed an attestation paper and swore to his age, without that recruiting officer being guilty of assisting in a perjury. I could understand it if the hoy were 17 or so, but this kind of thing has been going on to such an extent that I cannot but believe that there has been connivance on the part of the recruiting officers.

When did he join
the forces?

I have only this newspaper item which I shall be glad to give to my hon. friend. I do not propose to introduce this young man's name here. Another instance was brought to my attention when a father came to see me in March last. His son had enlisted in a battalion on the, 12th of March this year. The boy was born

on the 7th of March 1902, and was consequently only a few days over fifteen. I have not seen the boy myself, but I understand from the father that he is quite a boy, with no appearance of eighteen. However, he was taken on, and his father came to see me about it. I drew up a declaration by the father setting out the proper age of the boy, and sent it to the officer commanding at Regina. Subsequently, I procured a certificate of birth from the register general of Ontario, which confirmed the information which the father had given me. The commanding officer wrote me in reply:
Sir,-I have the honour to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 22nd March on the above marginally noted subject.
This boy swore that he was horn on the 1st March 1899. Now he could hardly be ignorant of his age to the extent of three years, and the country has been put to some expense, and I would like to be perfectly satisfied that this boy is under age before granting his discharge. If this boy's father proves he is only fifteen years of age, he also proves that the boy committed perjury.
Awaiting your further information on this subject, etc.
I understand that the boy .signed some paper, but he did not fully appreciate what he was doing. He certainly did not understand that he w.as swearing to something that was not true. He belongs to a good family, and I am quite certain that if he had believed ho was doing anything more than was usually connived at by recruiting officers he would not have put himself in the position of being branded for the rest of his life as a perjurer, as this commanding officer attempts to do. When he wrote like that, 1 felt that this was not a subject for me to discuss with him, but to bring to tlhe minister's attention. When a commanding officer puts it up to a father that his son, barely over 15 years of age is guilty of perjury because the father asks for his discharge, he forgets that his own recruiting officer must have been guilty of connivance. 'I felt that the commanding officer was guilty of a most improper action in endeavouring to be an accessary to the perjury which was already committed. Perhaps the minister can tell u.s the extent to which the recruiting of men over age and under age has gone on, and perhaps give us figures as to the number of men who have been rejected because they were under age.

The first case that my hon. friend referred to occurred at Val-cartier, I think in the first contingent that went overseas. Perhaps, there was a little

more laxity in connection with that expedition than with later contingents. With regard to the enlistment of men under age, some may have known what they were doing and others may not, but the practice the department has invariably pursued has been to release any boy under age, upon application from his parents. This also applies to the enlistment of boys under age who have gone to England. When it is made clear that they are under age, they are returned to Canada, although under the law, after being enlisted for three months, we could hold them. It is difficult to know (just where to place the blame. I have known of boys under age getting in under false pretenses, if you choose to call it that, and it would never be known that they were under age until they were about to be sent overseas, and then it might De found out and they would be discharged. Or a boy under age might enlist during the winter and his age not become known until the next summer. I have no doubt that in some cases the parents have acted in collusion. In other cases boys have enlisted in spite of their parents. Some of these boys are quite as big at fifteen or sixteen as boys of eighteen, and very often boys of eighteen look under sixteen, but everybody knows that that is the case. Where large numbers of men are enlisting, and when there is great anxiety to get men into the ranks, possibly as great care is not taken as should be taken. Particularly does this apply to the early days of the war, with the unfortunate result that the country is put to some expense. I do not know whether we can go so far as to charge with perjury every boy under age who enlists, because I believe that many of them do not fully appreciate what they are signing. But, as I said, the invariable practice of the department has been to let these boys out when their age has been proved.

I am not objecting to the fact that boys under eighteen have enlisted. This Parliament has given its own judgment on the question, because in the Bill providing for conscription we have made the minimum age 20 years. As the minister says, there are many boys under 18 who are physically better fit than many others over that age. I do not object at all to those boys who have the enthusiasm and the physical ability joining the ranks, but what I do object to is the attempt on the part of the commanding officer to brand a man as a perjurer for the rest of his life

because he has signed an attestation declaring that he is of a certain age, when probably he was in ignorance of the full force of what he was doing.
I would like to ask the minister a question on a subject which has been discussed on more than one occasion. In doing so, I do not wish any reference I may make to it to be understood as casting reflections upon either members of this House or others who have gone overseas. I have been told that there are many officers in the Old Country who are simply hanging about, who decline to be reduced from the ranks to which they were originally appointed, yet they will not go to the front, and they will not come home. This has been a source of complaint and irritation to the young men who have been induced to go over, and who find that those who have been in charge of them are unwilling to expose their lives to the dangers which the privates are called upon to face. I think the country would like information as to the extent to which superior officers have not taken a lower rank in order to get to the front. I hope it is not to a very considerable extent. Perhaps the minister can tell us the number of colonels, say, who have gone from England into France with lower rank, and what lower rank they have taken? I trust it will be understood I do not make these remarks in any spirit of criticism, or with the idea that the men are not doing their duty.

I thought I had a letter in my possession from which I should like to quote an extract. I do not find it at the moment, however. This letter came to me with respect to a colonel who reverted to major. He was a naan of very high stand* ing, and he said he was very happy to be able to do it. As a matter of fact, a good many officers have reverted to lower rank. A great many lieutenants, for instance, have reverted to the rank of sergeant. My hon. friend is not quite right in saying that they will not go to France, and that they will not come back home. A number of the officers in England would be very glad to go to France if an opportunity offered.
Are those officers under pay in London?
Some of them are under pay.
Why should they be?
They are coming back 'to Canada all 'the time, and many of them are reventing to private life.
What have they done beyond going to London and staying there?

My hon. friend knows what they have done. They have raised regiments 'and ihattadijons in this country. Some of them have not been able to raise full battalions, but they did the best they could. They did .all the country asked them 'to do. When they reached England their regiments were broken up because of military necessity, iand' their men were drafted to fill up other regiments and to fill gaps at the front. Those officers are in a difficult position. They are not cowards at all. There are just as good men who have never had the privilege of going to the trenches to fight as there are in the trenches. The difficulty is our .system has resulted 'in surplus officers, who are reverting to civil life as fast as possible. It iis not their fault that they did not succeed in getting to the trenches, and I would not want the impression to go .abroad that these men have done anything else but their whole duty in trying to get to the front.
To what rank would the colonels and majors usually revert?
I suppose a colonel would revert to the rank of major, if he reverted, and I presume a major would revert to the rank of captain.

I met a young man who bad been through the battle of Vimy Ridge, and I understood from him that Colonel Norman Laing, who recruited the 65th from Saskatoon, waited in England for a good many months and finally Teverted to the rank of lieutenant. He
10 p.m. went to France and took part in the battle of Vimy Ridge.
He deserved a great deal of credit for that.
And I understood that he was the only colonel who had reverted to the rank of lieutenant and had gone across. Perhaps the minister could give us some information on that point.
I have not any information on-the point at the moment. I am very sorry.

I am very pleased to have an opportunity of mentioning Colonel Norman Laing's name in this connection. He is 'a personal friend of mine land it is altogether to his credit that he took the action that he did.

Can the minister give u-3 'Same information about Mr. Olivar Asseiin? I understand he enlisted as a miajoT in Montreal. If it is not a secret, I would like to know whether he has reverted to a lower rank, and where he is now?
He is still a major.
Is he 'at the front?
He has been in the hospital for the last month or so.
Wounded?
No, he is ill.

I took up the case the other day of a young man who is under age, but who is in England with a signal corps. His father had a very serious accident and the another wants the hoy home. I tt'iik the deputy minister wrote to me that he had written to England. If it is possible to do anything to expedite the matter' I should be glad, as the people are now in their haying and anxious to gei the hoy home.

In regard to the matter of the reversion of officers to lower ranks in order to get to the front, when I first heard of this practice I thought it was a hardship; but on consideration I can see that it is in many cases only fair and is decidedly in the interest of the men in the trenches. A man may have been connected with the militia for years, going out for twelve days annually for drill and rising to the rank of major or colonel. He raises a Tegiment and goes overseas with it. It may be better that such a man, who has had no actual experience of modem warfare, *should be asked to revert to the rank of lieutenant or captain, as otherwise he might be placed in command of men who had been in the trenches for a year or a year and a half and had fought their way up to, -say, the rank of captain. Certainly the men 'in the trenches would ibe much safer under the command of the experienced fighter. But, while saying this,- I believe that in 'such cases the allowance paid to-the officer's family should not be reduced to those of the rank to which he reverts.
That is the regulation.
I did not know that.

The passports come under the Under Secretary of State for External Affairs. The rules and regulations are laid down by the British Government, and we have acted upon them. Duly qualified nurses are allowed to go over and there are extreme cases where others have gone. A lady came to my office to enlist my sympathy in respect to getting overseas, but the Under Secretary of State turned her down and she did not go. I do not think there is any question of influence about the matter, and I do not know of any favouritism. The rules are very stringent, and there are many women over there now who would be better in Canada; and it is not desirable that any women should go to England unless the circumstances are very serious indeed.

The minister will acquit me of any thought of accusing him of favouritism, but evidently, from what the minister says, there are cases which the Government, through the Secretary of State's Department, recognizes as exceptional. The minister knows enough about ladies to know that every lady thinks her case is exceptional. If not he has a great deal to learn. There is a danger, if the minister is not able to assure me that the rule is never broken, that these ladies will think that I am unable to get them the dispensation which somebody has secured for these other ladies. What would the minister call exceptional circumstances? If a lady's extreme passion is to be by the side of her husband, would that be considered an exceptional circumstance? Or would it

be so considered if she had an idea that the husband's charms may be lavished on some other woman and she ought to get over there-or what would he call exceptional circumstances? I ask the question very seriously.

I know of one case where a lady went over to get married, the idea being that it was desirable that as many ladies should be married in war times as possible, provided the matches were suitable ones. These people had been engaged for about two years or more. It was a bona fide case, and the lady was given a passport to go over. Has my hon. friend anybody in mind who wants to get married?
I have a case.

It is a very common predicament. I think the Government will find they are adding to the problems of the war very much ilf they take on themselves to decide what marriages are desirable and what are not. But if the 'minister has the personal gift and is able to constitute himself a successful match-maker, we are fortunate indeed in having such a minister. But still I do not quite understand the situation. The minister might tell us what he considers exceptional circumstances. I am not going to tell the affairs of the ladies with whom I have the honour of an acquaintance, but they have far stronger reasons than those given Iby the minister. The minister's case is a very ordinary one, for it is very common for a girl to want to marry an officer after he leaves for England, and I should think exceptional cases would be very frequent. Perhaps the minister would give me the information. This is Teally a matter associated with the war, and therefore under the Militia Department. Under what circumstances would wives be permitted to go to their husbands?

They often go
over when their husbands have nothing to do with military affairs.

The minister has given
me something I have been waiting for for some time, the exceptional case. A case came under my notice such as he described, where the passports had been given. An officer engaged to a young lady on this side of the water anticipated getting married in a month or two, but was called to go across. When he got to England he found he was likely to remain some time, and cabled for the young lady to come over, but I was unable to obtain a passport. The circumstances were such as outlined by the minister. I could give all the necessary requirements to make this an exceptional case, if there is such a thing, but what I was interested in was the answer given to the hon. gentleman from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) as to the pension and pay of the officers. I imagine a number of officers would be more inclined to revert if they thought their pay, and the amount given to their families, would not revert at the same time. A number of officers in England can get to the front by reverting. They are not unwilling to revert, as I understand it, but it will leave their families and themselves in a very bad predicament, owing to the reduced pay which they and their families will receive. I know several cases of that kind. I had a letter this week from a young man who left his family and went over, and has been there for some time, and he said he would not mind reverting at all, but would not like? to see his family on the road, and he is not a man who would take anything from the Patriotic Fund-die does not feel like doing that. In 1914, when this matter was being discussed, I put the question to the Prime Minister, perhaps in a little different form. I asked him the question: if a man goes overseas as a captain or major, and over there takes a lower rank, would his pay be for the lower rank, and would the pension to his family be according to the lower rank? The Prime Minister gave me an affirmative answer in both cases. That was his opinion at that time. If there are different regulations since, I think it would be in the public interest that we should all know about them. Suppose a man is a captain in England and can only get to the front by reverting to a lieutenancy. What pay will he get if he reverts, and what amount will his family get? Will the pay remain that of a captain, or will it be reduced to that of a lieutenant?

The pay will be
the pay of the rank to which he reverts, but the separation allowance, in the case of a married man, will be the same as if he had not reverted, and the pension would be the same-according to the higher rank. If he reverted from captain to lieutenant, he would get lieutenant's pay, but, if he is a married man, the separation allowance would be that of a captain, and his pension would be that of a captain.

The difference to his
family would be the difference in the assigned pay, practically, because he would
399S

not be able to assign as much of his pay to his family under the lower rank as he would under the higher.

I would like to know if
the position is still as it was some months ago in regard to non-commissioned officers who are members of battalions which have been broken up and sent over to France. Some time ago the condition was this: noncommissioned officers were all compelled to revert to the rank of privates, and lost their pay as non-commissioned officers, and their opportunity for pensions. I would like to know if that is still the position?

The situation inregard to that is the same as the situation in regard to the question raised by my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham). The pay is that of the lower rank, and the separation and pension that of the higher rank.
How long is it since this latter arrangement was given effect to?
About six months ago.
In the case I refer to, these men reverted more than six months ago, but I got the information from them less than six months ago. Would that new condition be retroactive?
Yes, it would be retroactive.

The instance I mentioned here was that of a battalion sergeant-major, who, when he went to the front, took the rank of private, and took the private's pay, when he thought he was- getting a continuation of the sergeant-major's regimental pay. When he was wounded, and came back and was boarded to be sent back to Canada, he found out that, instead of having money coming to him, he was in debt. Would that retroactive pay be of any benefit to this man?
I am afraid the sergeant-major misunderstood the regulations in that case.
I understand the minister to say that the non-commissioned officer who now reverts on going to France receives the pay of his former rank?
Receives the pay of the rank to which he Teverts.

He was a battalion sergeant-major, and became a private, and he understood his pay as battalion sergeant-

major was continued. He had been drawing his battalion sergeant-major pay after he was wounded, but when he was settled up with, to be sent back to Canada, he found, instead of being a comfortable sum of money ahead, he was actually in debt to the department. Will the new regulation be retroactive to the benefit of that man?

The regulation would give him the pay of a private. Unfortunately he had been drawing the higher pay, and when the books were balanced he found himself in debt. That was the unfortunate situation. Nevertheless, when a man reverts he gets the pay of the rank to which he reverts. The separation allowance and pension, however, are of the higher rank from which he has reverted.
He will get the pension of a battalion -sergeant-major?
Yes.
Although he was in the position -of -a private when he was wounded?
Yes. And the separation iaillowan.ee, if he is a married mian, would be of the higher rank.
He was not a married -man, but he had a dependent mother -at the ti-m-e.
The -separation 'allowance could have gone to the dependent -mother at the pay f-o the higher /rank, if the father was not living.

Why iis it necessary that the non-commissioned officer should become a private upon going to France? His position -is different from that of the commissioned officer, especially of the battalion commissioned officer. The battalion commissioned officer loses his rank because he is not in -comm-and of -a sufficient number of men to warrant his retaining it. But the non-commissioned officer goes with the draft of the battalion to which he belongs; he goes with the men with whom he was associated -as non-commissioned officer. I am at a loss -to know why, under normal conditions, a non-commissioned officer should be degraded -to the position of private when he goes to France.
Of course, he is not forced to do it. There is only one sergeant-major in a battalion.
I was not speaking of -a battalion -sergeant-major; I was -speaking of the ordinary sergeant or corporal.
Why should they have to revert? When a platoon is going to France, why should not the non-commissioned officers who accompany that platoon retain their rank?

There may be a surplus of certain grades of non-commissioned officers. Moreover, these men may be anxious to get to the front as soon as possible, and their anxiety is such that they are willing to go as privates rather than wait until some other opportunity occurs. They are not forced to revert in rank.

I understand that they are compelled to go; that it is not a matter of option with them. The non-commissioned officer is not in the position of an officer; he must go if he is sent. That is to say, the rank that he has attained and the pay that he has been receiving are taken from him without good reason. In a case like that I think it would be fair to adopt the suggestion that the member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) made in connection with commissioned officers: that the pay and allowances of the non-commissioned officer who, for reasons over which he has no control, is compelled to serve as a private, should be continued.

I should like to put in a word again in support of the member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliyer). I am sorry to have to say to the minister that he is not quite informed about what they do with non-commissioned officers in England. The non-commissioned officer when he goes to England is treated very harshly indeed. As the hon. member for Edmonton says, he has no option at all; he automatically becomes a private.
Originally the non-commissioned officers went to England as acting non-commissioned officers, and if they were found to be qualified and to be fit in every way to hold their rank, they were confirmed in that rank in England. But because there was a surplus of non-commissioned officers, a large number having accumulated in England, they made the harsh rule that in future no noncommissioned ranks should be confirmed in England, and that upon their arrival in England these non-commissioned officers should become privates, no matter what
their qualifications were. When the minister remembers that the qualifications of a sergeant are the same as those of a lieutenant, that the examinations are identical and that the certificate is obtained in Canada largely through the enterprise and at the expense of the non-commissioned officer, he will realize that a very great injustice is done to these men and that when they go over they should not be obliged merely to take a chance upon their getting their rank back again. When I was told that these non-commissioned officers could go across to France as privates and that, if they were eligible for promotion, they could very easily get that promotion in the field, I inquired whether any steps were taken to ensure that that promotion should come to them in the field; whether, for instance, any lists of qualified non-commissioned officers were sent over to France. The answer came from headquarters in London, through the department here, that no such lists were sent over; that it was left entirely to chance whether the qualifications of these men were ever recognized.
I want to mention another instance which has occurred in connection with the reverting in rank of non-commissioned officers. We are told that if they are killed, the pensions paid to their widows are continued at the rate for non-commissioned officers. It is quite true that there is an order in council directing that their pensions shall so continue. But we have in Canada a Pensions Board which, so far as my experience with it is concerned is not much troubled about orders in council. It seems to act upon the principle that the widow of a noncommissioned officer gets only what she can prove she is entitled to get, and if she has no friends, lives a long way from here or is not in a position to put up proof, she gets the very lowest amount that the Pensions Board can give her, which is the pension of the wife of a private soldier. I have a case of that kind before the Pensions Board now. As- commanding officer of a deceased sergeant, I have submitted to the board all the proof possible and have referred them to headquarters here for absolute proof. The hoard, however, have declined to recognize the widow's claim because the Record Office in London persists in telling her that this man died as a private. It is quite true that he died ae a private, but he had before him the guarantee of this Government under order ini council that if he died as a private his widow would be pensioned as the widow of a sergeant. I cannot make the Pensions Board

recognize this fact. They simply keep travelling around in a circle, like the old Circumlocution Office, and they come back after a series of letters to the assertion that the Record Office says that the man died as a private and that his widow is to get the pension of a private's widow. I have deferred taking this matter up in the House because there is a resolution on the Order Paper dealing with the Pensions Board, and I thought that the proper time to take up a matter of this kind was upon the consideration of that resolution. But in case that resolution is never reached, I should like to call the minister's attention to the necessity for seeing not only that when noncommissioned officers get to England they get some advantage for the qualifications they secured here, but that the Pensions Board shall be made to. recognize the contract of this Government with the soldiers and their widows.
An ordeT in council in respect to a matter of that kind has to be obeyed by the Pensions Board.
But they do not obey it.

I understand the member for New Westminster (Mr. Taylor) to say that the difficulties thrown in the way make it impossible to grant the pension as he suggested; at least, he has a case of that kind in mir.d.
I will ask my deputy to draw the attention of the Pension Board to this matter again to see what their answer is to the arguments put forward here by my .hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) laud my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. Taylor).

In this connection, it was drawn to my attention by the men with whom I conversed that the non-commissioned officers at the base in England, who remained there in comfort and safety, retained rank and pay, while the non-commissioned officer who went to the front and risked (his life and did the flighting, went as a private. That is neither fair nor reasonable, and I hope the minister will take some means of adjusting the matter so that a man will not be penalized because of the service he renders.
I shall be glad to take up that matter also.

When an officer reverts to. a lower rank, is there any one to tell him what his pay is going to he at the time of reversion? A few days ago I

brought to the notice of the department a case somewhat in line with what the hon. member for Edmonton has said. It seemed to. me to be a case of very great hardship. W^hemone o'f our best young men from the Six Nations tribe, who had served with distinction for the past two years and won the Military Cross and several other horn ours on the field, got 'honih a short time ago, he was informed that he had been overpaid during the three years of his reversion of rank in England to the extent of about $317, and his pay and his wife's separation allowance were stopped until the $317 was made up. I wrote the department stating that this seemed to 'be an extreme ease of hardship. I think steps have been taken to adjust the matter, buit a case of that kind should not occur. I am not (blaming the minister at all, because I 'believe such cases occur on the other slide. But when an officer reverts in rank to a lower grade, there should be some one to tell him at the time what his pay is going to be. It is not right to send a man in a bill for money spen t during three years, and I hope that will not occur in many cases. I have had to deal with other cases of hardship in regard to pensions. This is perhaps not the proper time to 'bring up such questions, but tlie Government should -be more liberal in the matters of pensions, especially to the lower ranks.
It does not seem to be right to ask a widow to swear that an only son was her sole support, and to provide that unless she does so she cannot get anything. I had a case of that kind a few days ago. A widow had lost her only son. She had taken some bank work and because she was doing this work, it was proposed that she should receive no allowance whatever, although her only son had been killed at the front and her husband had been dead for some years. Whoever is in authority in those matters should be a little more liberal. When an officer reverts to a lower grade,^as many have done in order to get to the front, he should have a distinct understanding when he leaves for the front on what basis he is to be paid and what separation allowance 'his wife and family are to receive. The minister probably knows the name of the man whose case I have mentioned. I have mentioned it to him on a previous occasion.	[DOT]

These unfortunate questions of overpayment occur now and again. I think this man's name was Smith, but the matter is being adjusted. The Min-

ister of Finance is the responsible minister in Tegard to pensions. That question does not oome up under these estimates.

Will 'the minister
tell us whether the Minister of Finance intends going on with his resolution in regard to pensions? It has stood on the OrdeT Paper for a long time. It was understood at the time it was put on the Order Paper that the matter was to be referred to a special committee, as was done last year. As we are nearing the end of the session, it is desirable that the matter should be brought up at once, because in all parts of the country questions are being brought up in regard to inequalities of pensions.

The Minister of
Finance was in the House a few moments ago. If my hon. friend or some other hon. member will ask him when he comes in again, he will probably be able to give an answer to the question.

I understand that when I was out of the chamber a little while ago, there was some discussion about soldiers'under the age of eighteen years serving in the ranks. I have had two cases drawn to my attention in the last few days. I have sent them forward to the deputy minister and he has been kind enough to say that he will forward them to the authorities on the other side. One of those cases was a boy whose date of birth is the 3rd day of June, 1901, so that he would be sixteen years old on the 3rd day of June this year. This boy, I am told by his parents who live in my constituency, is in France at the present time. His brother was killed in France some time in May. This boy is very young and his parents are anxious about him. His father was away from home at the time the boy enlisted, otherwise, I do not think he would have been permitted to enlist. The other case is from the same district. The young fellow was born on the 15th of November, 1900, so that he would be about sixteen years and eight months old. I understand this young fellow is in Witley camp, Surrey, England. I can give the names and numbers of these soldiers, but it is not necessary that I should do so. What is the policy of the department in regard to these boys? Is it possible to order this boy in France back under the circumstances? If so, that ought to be done because he is altogether too young for active service. The other boy who is in England is not quite in the same position, because he is a little
older, but in both cases their parents are applying to have them returned. Is it possible to have that done?

We had this question up while my hon. friend was out of the chamber. It has been the policy to discharge all the young men under age. As soon as our attention is directed to a case, we get the birth certificate or other proper evidence of birth. It is difficult to know on whom to place the blame. Sometimes the fault is the boy's; sometimes it is the parents'. We refer to England demands for discharge of boys who are under age. My hon. friend refers to one boy in France.
I do not suppose that the parents made an application to have the boy taken out of the ranks while he was in Canada. They sometimes delay making application.
I understand that they wrote some letters about him to the department when he was at Aldershot, but nothing was done, and then they wrote me.

If my Ihon. friend will forward the data to my deputy, or to the department, and will enclose a birth certificate-there is very little difficulty, as a rule, in getting that-we will have it forwarded overseas.

I want to call the minister's attention to a condition prevailing at Halifax, and which, perhaps, is not to be found anywhere else in Canada, There, since the beginning of the war, two local regiments have been doing duty at the forts. I am not sure whether the full strength of the regiments are so engaged, but I think that is probable. As I understand it, these men do not receive the separation 'allowance.
They are a part of the garrison 'at Halifax, are they not?
I suppose so.
Did they not take the place of the permanent force who went overseas?

I think so, but, of course, the garrison duties have been greatly increased since then. These regiments are engaged at McNab's Island, York Redoubt, and such points as that. To all intents and purposes, they are in the same' position as if they were serving overseas, as they have to give up their work and are unable to live at home. I think these men should be granted the separation allowance.
The 'married men get 45 cents a.day subsistence 'allowance.
Many of these men have represented to ime that they should receive the separation allowance.
Do their families live at Halifax?

They would, but the men are unable to live at home, and are unable to carry on their ordinary business. I would like the minister to give this matter some consideration, because I think .a great deal can be said 'in favour of 'these men being paid the usual separation allowance, and I certainly think they should 'receive it.
The subsistence allowance for married men amounts to $13.50 a month. The separation allowance is $20 a month.

I was not aware that the subsistence allowance was so large. At all events, I submit that these men are entitled to the full separation allowance. The case of such men is rather different from that of the forces doing duty almost anywhere else in Canada. They are constantly on duty; they have to give up their ordinary work, and, furthermore, they cannot escape this duty, because they are called out. I really do think that they are entitled to the ordinary separation allowance.

I confess I have never been able to understand why this distinction is made between the subsistence allowance and the separation allowance. I am not a military man, and there are many things in the military line that I do not understand. There may be a good reason for this distinction, but it seems to me that a married man who is separated from his family, even if he is only doing garrison duty at Halifax or some other part of the country, should receive the $20 separation allowance instead of the 45 cents a day subsistence.

The regulations in regard to this matter have been in force since the war began. I think hon. gentlemen will agree that there is some difference between the man who enlists for service in the city of Halifax, where he is in touch with his family, and to some extent, perhaps, with his ordinary business, and where he has a guiding hand over his family affairs, and the man who goes into the

trenches and undertakes all the hazards of warfare as it is carried on in France and Belgium to-day. I might point out that the 45 cents a day subsistence allowance is what the permanent force were getting whose place these men took.

But they were volunteers. In the case I am referring to, the two local regiments were called out, and they could not avoid doing duty; that distinction should be taken into consideration. They were called out, I suppose, under the authority of the Militia Council or some other body. I trust the minister will promise me to give the matter some consideration.
I wish to call the minister's attention te .another matter, and perhaps I can best illustrate by giving the facts of one case. A Canadian, soldier went overseas as an officer, and for some reason was courtmartialed and degraded. Later on he joined a British regiment as a private. The department continued to pay the separation allowance to his wife, who was residing in Halifax, without knowledge of his having left the Canadian service, and in this way some $300 or more was paid to her. Subsequently the department's attention was called to the fact, I think by myself, that this man had ceased to be a member of the Canadian force. Regularly since then the wife of this man receives a notice from some branch of the Militia Department requesting her to refund the amount that was improperly paid to her. The amounts were undoubtedly received and used by her in good faith.	There are no doubt a
great many cases of this kind; I have heard some of my fellow-members speak of them, and I would like to know what the policy of the department is in regard to such claims. In most cases it will be found utterly impossible to collect them. It seems to me that it means a great deal of labour on the part of some officials of the department to be sending out these notices regularly, without much hope of accomplishing anything. If bona fides can be established, if it can be shown that there was no fraud, I think the Government might as well abandon their claims on these women and wipe the accounts off the slate altogether.

There have been quite a number of cases where men are far away from their homes and their families, and they are discharged, or something happens to them, and the wife or the one

to whom the separation allowance is assigned, draws it; but, they are not all innocent. When they endorse the cheques, they have to certify that the husband is still serving in the forces. This is printed in good plain English on the backs of the cheques, and they read it at the time of en-dorsation. No doubt there are cases of hardship, but it is very difficult for me to make a statement here that the Government would be permitted to forgive all claims of that kind, because if I did so it would be unfair and unjust, for the reason that most of those claims -arise in respect of people who know what they are doing when they endorse the cheques.
Do I understand the minister to say he will be able to give the House the figures as to the unfit men who were in England, and those who have been returned to Canada?
Yes.
I am speaking of those who were unfit when they enlisted, not those who became unfit after enlistment, such as the list I gave the House to-night.

I cannot see how you could trace out a thing of that kind. How can you get a statement showing that the men who might have been returned from Great Britain were medically unfit when they enlisted? I can assure my hon. friend from Edmonton that I have, since I have been minister, exerted myself to give any information desired by the committee or the House and I shall continue to do so, but in regard to this particular point I do not see how it is possible to get the information. If I thought the information could be obtained I would certainly undertake to obtain it, and bring it down to-morrow; but, as I say, I cannot see how it can be done.
Of course, it is not for me to say how it can be done. At the same time, I should imagine the medical records would be complete.
I will look into it to-morrow morning, and if the hon. member for Edmonton will draw my attention to it again I will give him a further statement. If the information can be obtained he shall have it.

In view of the statements in the Bruce, the Baibtie and the Jones reports, this is the most important statement the Government can place before Parliament with reference to the cost of the war and the efficiency of the work done. We
are informed that there- have been enlisted and gone overseas, or are enlisted for overseas service in Canada about 340,000 or
350.000	men. Those are our effective enlistments. I believe we have 130,000 men in Prance. We have had in the neighbourhood of 100,000 casualties, of which I suppose it would not ibe unreasonable to say that possibly twenty-five per cent would not be permanent, which would leave about
75.000	as permanently disabled. In other words we have 130,000 men in France,
75,000	permanent casualties,
11 p.m. making 205,000 effective men ac-* counted for out of 340,000 or
350.000	enlisted. There are still 135,000 men to be taken into consideration. How many of those 135,000 are available for service in France? Because, we must remember we are not fighting this war in Canada nor in England. We are fighting it in France, and it is only the man who is able to fight in France who- is of military value to the Dominion of Canada. Either those 135,000 men are not of military value to Canada, and should not be on the pay list-
They are all being made use of in England or in France.

I do not think the minister is absolutely accurate when he says they are all being made use of. I understand from these reports that there is an effort to keep them in employment as an excuse for their being on the paylist. That is not what we should -be trying to do. We are trying to put men on the fighting line in France to keep them there, and to support them there. If we have 135,000 men who have not been on the fighting line we want to know whether they are fit to go or not, and whether they are a force we can Tely on to reach the front ultimately. The reports of those commissions certainly throw very grave doubt on the efficiency of an unknown proportion of that 135,000 men. We need those men. -So. far as we know they are industrially efficient. If they are not fit for France they are fit for Canada, and they should be either in France or in Canada, or perhaps in England -simply on the way to France. I urge upon the minister that the question I have asked him is a most important question to the people of Canada, as fixing their position in this war, and as to what they have done and what they are able to do. In the past we have deluded ourselves by speaking of the number of men enlisted, when, as a matter of fact, of those nominally enlisted 75,000 were not in service or were found to be un-



fit after enlistment, and left the service. We were not doing ourselves or our cause any good 'by claiming an enlistment of 418,000, when we really-had an ,effective enlistment of a little less than 350,000. We were not doing ourselves any good by claiming an enlistment of 350,000 it, as a matter of fact, a considerable proportion of that number is not fit for the firing line, which is the only place we need soldiers. Any place else a great deal of the work can be done by stenographers or people who are militarily unfit; but we do not want to have to make a pretense of having raised an army of 350,000 men if any such proportion of them as these reports indicate are unfit for the firing line. Let us get down to business and know what we have done, what we can do, and admit that we have not done what we have not done.

Like the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) I should like to ascertain how many unfit men were permitted to enlist. The statement of the minister ,is absolutely true, that neither he nor any other man can give the number of men who were unfit when they enlisted; that is absolutely out of the question. In southern Manitoba when the battalions were being enlisted in small towns

and by this means eight or ten battalions were raised that would not otherwise have been raised-the men were examined by the local doctors. It. is true that these doctors were inexperienced in that kind of work, but I believe they did the work honestly, and I can use no better word. The men from Manitoba were gathered at Camp Hughes and there they began their training. The camp had not been running for two- months before a board of three members of the Army Mediical 'Service visited it. The men were stripped, and I believe honestly examined to the very best of the ability of this board, who were as efficient as any three man who- could be found. Some men were discharged. These doctors who discarded these men could not say whether they were unfit when they enlisted. As a medical .man, I am prepared to make the declaration, and I challenge contradiction, that it would be impossible for the hoard to affirm that many of those men were unfit when they enlisted. The battalions went on drilling, and in the fall, before being transported overseas, they were again inspected by a mediical board and still more men were discarded. They went overseas, and before being transported to France were again examined and .more men discarded. It would 'be impossible for the Minister of 
Militia ox any other man to say how many of them were unfit when they enlisted.

The minister has brought
down a full statement of the discharges of men in Canada. There should be no serious difficulty in giving an equally full statement about the discharges in England before the troops go- to France.
I understood the bon. member to ask the minister to give the number of men who were unfit when they were enlisted. That is impossible.

The minister has given
the number of men who were unfit when they enlisted but who were discharged in Canada. I whs endeavouring to secure a detailed statement of those who were discharged for like causes after their arrival in England.

I think the hon.
member for Souris (Mr. Schaffner) is quite right. These battalions have gone before boards more than once. They were weeded out and weeded out until they were almost disheartened. Then in England more of them were set aside as not fit to go to France. My bon. friend (Mr. Oliver) is under the impression that quite a number of these men might be returned to Canada for industrial employment. There are very few men who are not doing some military duty in England that would have to be^one by a man who was fit for the trenches if they were not doing it. We cannot get those men back. I have had relatives ask for the return of men' who are doing police duty, but they will not let them come back. They are as necessary for that work as they would be for work in the trenches. There is no such surplus of rank and file in England as my hon. friend thinks. There is no surplus at all. If men went over in the earlier stages of the war who were unfit for service, they would have been returned long ago unless they were usefully employed.

I have given the count as it has been given to me of the number of men we have. We should have 135,000 men available f-or the firing line. We are told we have no such number. I forget what the number is, but we are supposed to have something like fifteen or twenty thousand men in England fit for the firing line. What is the condition of the rest? If they are not fit for the firing line, why are they there?

They are being
prepared for the firing line. They get far

more intensive training in England than in this country. Training has. undergone an evolution since the war began. They are giving more intensive training now, and preparing men foT category A, working up all the time.

What proportion of the
135,000	men does the hon minister think are fit for the firing line, or will become fit?
Out of the 126,241 there were 7,981 officers, 26,359 in Category Al, fit for the firing line. .
Which" means what?

Perfectly fit for France. There were 26,927 in A2 almost ready for France. There were 5,147 in A3, the next class. Then we come to A4, 383 under 18 years of age, and 3,086 over 18. I do not know what that means. Then we come to Category B, which has three classes. Category B is the class training men to get into Category A. I have before me the exact particulars, in a very long and complicated document, explaining how this 126,241 gradually, as far as possible, get into Category A. Of that number there was a large number in hospitals. I think this table appears in the Prime Minister's speech on the Military Service Bill, and will be found in Hansard.

I am constantly in receipt of requests from the parents of soldiers overseas, asking if their sons could not obtain leave of absence. In most cases they are men who have, been wounded, or who have been on duty overseas almost since the beginning of the war, and who, for apparently very strong reasons, would be entitled to a leave of absence. I suppose every member of the House receives some similar request, and it is impossible to trouble the department each time with each particular case, and I would like to have from the minister, if possible, some declaration of departmental policy in respect to this matter. In many cases my correspondent will refer to the fact that in his or her locality there is some officer, or man who has returned from overseas on leave of absence, and naturally they think his case was not so deserving as their own. Upon that, of course, there may be a great difference of opinion, but there is a feeling on the part of interested persons that there is some partiality shown in giving leave of absence to certain officers and pri-254J
vates. I am sure I need not elaborate the idea, because the department probably have similar cases before it more than once every day. It may be impossible to make a statement of policy upon a matter of this kind, because cases may differ very much, but I should like to know the ground upon which leave of absence is secured on behalf of any person overseas.
SiT EDWARD KEMP: The applications are more numerous every day, I think. There are various reasons given for asking that relatives be returned to Canada. The question is a very difficult one to handle. My hon. friend will understand that occasionally a very sincere ,and affectionate father or mother will chaTge favouritism in certain circumstances. There is no isueh thing as favouritism in the matter.
By whom is it determined?

By the necessities of the troops in France. A man who has had sick leave is frequently returned to Canada to convalesce, and if his recovery can go on as well in Canada as in England, or elsewhere, he is allowed to come out. A board can examine him in Canada, to find out whether or not he is fit to go back to the front, and if he is not fit his leave can be extended on the recommendation of the Military Medical Board. There are requests made to us on account of the father or mother being 'ill, or one or the other having died, or some financial trouble. In an army of three or four hundred thousand men there are tragedies happening every day-every hour of the day-in respect of their relatives who are behind them. In a city of three hundred thousand people there are many accidents happening every day, and many pathetic incidents. All these things are reflected on the department, to a certain extent, in the prosecution of the war. The requests are very numerous, and we answer all of them, whether verbal or written. These requests are usually written, and it is desirable they should be in writing, so that they may be investigated, but where a man is medically fit for his duties as 'a soldier just at the present time, it is very, very difficult to get any leave of absence. Sometimes the relatives of soldiers in Canada make application to have their sons returned to Canada when the sons do not want to be treated in this way, *and it is very embarassing for the man to be told he has bqen granited leave. He does not like to leave his comrades. He is

singled out 'as a .man *who wants to get away and obtain some preference over the others. It is .a difficult matter to 'handle. On the 1st of February, 1917, I issued a circular which at that time and 'at the present *time covers nearly 'all the different forms -of requisitions that are made for the return -of soldiers from the front. There are ten iin all.
It shows the procedure which ought to be taken in each case; I will send a copy of it over to my hon. friend. They are used every day in the department.
Who is the ultimate judge of the matter? The commanding officer of the battalion in which the applicant is enlisted?

The proper way to proceed is for the applicant himself to make application through his commanding officer at the front; then the case is rested on a solid foundation. But unless there are excellent reasons why it should be granted, the leave of absence is not granted to a man who is physically fit for his duties in France or in England. I do not know of any cases in which such requests have been granted, unless it has been in the case of men under medical treatment who can pass -through their period of convalescence here as well as they can in England. Many persons who have occasion to receive applications of the kind to which my hon. friend refers ask the Militia Department to furnish them with copies of this circular in order that they may be able to answer the many questions that they get in respect to the return of soldiers.

I know several cases of men who enlisted for overseas service, were passed by the local doctor, but, when the battalion came to go overseas, were directed by the Medical Board to remain at home because they were not medically -fit to go across. In some cases these men were drafted into home defence battalions.
I 'have in mind several coal miners who were perfectly willing to go across, but who were compelled under these conditions to remain in Halifax in a home defence unit. They have no interest or heart in their work, and they want to get back home.
I have also in mind the case of a coal miner who enlisted in some unit which is now at Camp Borden, but who was declared medically unfit on account of heart disease. He has been retained in the service, but of course he has lost all interest in his work and is anxious to get back to his mine.
Is he doing home, guard duty?

He enlisted in some unit which had to be sent to Camp Borden for training; evidently it was not an infantry unit. There does not seem to be much use in keeping men who have volunteered for overseas service but who have ultimately been found to be medically unfit. If the man to whom I refer particularly would be more useful in some occupation connected with the industrial life of the country, he ought to be allowed to go.
I have a question to ask with regard to separation allowances. A young man, the only support of his sister, volunteered to go overseas, and was assured by the recruiting officer that in the event of his going his sister would get separation allowance. A similar statement was made with regard to the Patriotic Fund-about which there is no misunderstanding in our province, because the local authorities deal with it. The young man went away and left his sister on the farm, but she got no separation allowance; she simply got the assigned pay. It seems to me that separation allowance ought to be extended to cover the case of a man who leaves behind a dependent-mother, father or sister, as the case may be. I have in mind also the case of an officer who went overseas. He had married a very respectable lady. I do not know what could^have gone wrong, but he refused to authorize her to receive the assigned pay. She has a family. Is any parental authority exercised by the department to cover cases where men who go to the front do not provide for those whom they leave behind? One more question: Is the recruiting throughout the country being main-taFned, and will it be maintained in its present state? .	[DOT]
